articles.title: Exposure to Sexualised Appearance and Beauty Content on Social Media and Body Satisfaction in Female Adolescents: A Computational Real-World Approach
articles.authors: Christina Haag; Mingyue Zha; Matti Vuorre; Laura Boeschoten; Amanda M Ferguson; Sebastian Kurten; Amelia Leyland-Craggs; Valerie Yap; Jasmine Fardouly; Amy Orben
articles.abstract: Experimental studies show that viewing idealised bodies on social media can lower body satisfaction, but whether this extends to the content adolescents actually encounter is unknown, because studies of everyday exposure have relied on self-report rather than on what was actually viewed. In an observational study, we combined TikTok data donation with a 14-day ecological momentary assessment in 66 female adolescents aged 14–18. A locally run computer vision pipeline classified the visual content of 242,422 watched videos for thin and sexualised female bodies – coding the imagery itself rather than hashtags or captions – and metadata-based classifiers identified beauty-filter use and TikTok’s own beauty-related content labels. Content meeting the body criterion made up under one minute of roughly 91 watched minutes per day. Across all three measures, daily exposure was not associated with end-of-day body satisfaction, within or between persons, nor was morning body satisfaction associated with subsequent exposure. Everyday exposure to appearance ideals may be too sparse and too stable from day to day for day-level designs to detect any effect of it.

articles.title: Selective Exposure to Environmental Messages: Dual Sentiment Pathways to Information-Seeking Intentions
articles.authors: Changyu Jing; Suzanne Oosterwijk; Disa Sauter
articles.abstract: Environmental problems are intensifying, prompting expanded public communication efforts to raise awareness and motivate pro-environmental behavior. However, meaningful engagement with environmental messages is often selective, as people actively choose among many competing messages. In this paper, we examined how active engagement with environmental messages related to affective orientations (i.e., sentiments) towards environmental issues. Through a selective exposure paradigm, participants selected from four types of environmental messages varying in valence (positive vs. negative) and personal relevance (human vs. animal). We expected that engagement with these messages would be associated with changes in hopeful and anxious sentiments toward environmental issues. These sentiment shifts, in turn, were expected to predict the likelihood of participants seeking further environmental information. In an initial exploratory study (N = 283), participants’ selection of the different kinds of environmental messages showed no direct effect on environmental information-seeking intentions. Further analyses revealed two competing indirect paths: (a) increased seeking intentions via enhanced anxious sentiments and (b) reduced seeking intentions via diminished hopeful sentiments. These patterns were replicated in a confirmatory study (N = 1,009), demonstrating their robustness. Together, these findings suggest that the effectiveness of environmental communication is not limited to valence-congruent sentiments. Instead, the balance of emotional reactions that messages trigger shapes information-seeking behavior.

articles.title: Healing campuses: Implementing Nature-Based Interventions to Promote University Student Mental Health and Wellbeing
articles.authors: Melissa O’Shea; Brittany Patafio; David Skvarc; Cindy Zhou; hannah capon; Tracy Garvin; Nina Hunter; Claire Henderson-Wilson; Justin T Lawson; Dieter Kotte
articles.abstract: Innovative and accessible strategies are needed to address mental health burden among university students. Nature-based interventions (NBIs), which involve therapeutic activities conducted in nature spaces, are emerging to promote student wellbeing on university campuses. This review examined the range of NBIs implemented within universities and their reported benefits using a systematic search and narrative synthesis methodology. Evidence was searched from database inception to August 2026, identifying twelve studies representing eleven trials across five countries. Interventions involved forest therapy (n=5), mindfulness-based programs (n=4) adapted for outdoor campus settings, and therapeutic horticulture interventions (n=3). Evidence suggests that forest therapy is associated with reductions in stress and anxiety and improvements in mood, attention and overall wellbeing. Nature-integrated mindfulness programs were linked to reduced depressive symptoms, rumination, stress and anxiety, alongside enhanced wellbeing, mindfulness and connection to nature. Preliminary evidence suggests on campus therapeutic horticulture interventions may be associated with improvements in anxiety among university students and represent an accessible and affordable way to build nature and social connection. While findings are promising, evidence remains limited and of weak quality, highlighting the need for further robust research on implementation and sustainability within university contexts.

articles.title: Resting-state alpha scale-free dynamics predict individual differences in the balance between reward-learned and preference-based values during free choice
articles.authors: Jianhong Zhu; Junya Hashimoto; Tatsuru Honda; Kazuki Yamamoto; Mayo Anno; Georg Northoff; Takashi Nakao
articles.abstract: Values learned through reward can continue to influence choices guided by one's own preferences, such as which painting to hang, to an extent that varies across individuals. Because such preferences build up gradually across choices, their expression may depend on how well internally generated states are sustained over time, a property indexed by long-range temporal correlations (LRTC) in intrinsic brain activity. We tested whether resting-state alpha-band LRTC predicts individual differences in the balance between reward-learned and preference-based values. Eighty-one participants learned through probabilistic feedback which of four abstract shapes tended to be rewarded, and then judged their preferences among these shapes and 11 new shapes without feedback. Alpha LRTC was estimated by detrended fluctuation analysis of resting-state electroencephalography recorded before, between, and after the tasks. A trial-level mixed-effects model showed that reward history influenced preference judgments and that this influence decreased with resting-state alpha LRTC: participants with weak LRTC chose high-reward shapes over new shapes on 75% of trials, whereas those with strong LRTC were close to indifference (54%). The relationship was distributed across the scalp, stable across recordings, and not explained by spectral power or learning performance. Resting-state alpha LRTC is thus related to how strongly reward-learned values are carried into preference-based choice. Given the view that stronger LRTC reflects a longer window over which internally generated states are integrated, the observed relationship could arise because the window is biased toward values built up through one's own choices, or because it attenuates values learned under a criterion that no longer applies; which account holds remains to be determined.

articles.title: Accelerometer-Measured Activity and Psychological Well-Being in Older Adults: A Multilevel Longitudinal Analysis of NHATS Data
articles.authors: Kyungmi Lee; Jennifer B. Levin
articles.abstract:
Objectives: To examine whether objectively measured activity was associated with psychological well-being in older adults and whether social participation and digital connectivity were related to these associations.
Methods: Using three waves of accelerometer and survey data from the National Health and Aging Trends Study (2022–2024), this analysis applied multilevel models with within-between decomposition to examine three activity indicators (mean activity, relative amplitude, and behavioral fragmentation) and four well-being outcomes (loneliness, positive affect, meaning and purpose, and self-determination) in 543 participants. Between-person structural equation models examined social participation as a statistical correlate, and cross-level interactions tested digital connectivity as a moderator of within-person associations.
Results: At the between-person level, fragmentation was associated with three of four outcomes (positive affect, meaning and purpose, self-determination), whereas mean activity was associated with one (positive affect); seven of 24 coefficients survived Bonferroni correction. Mean activity showed within-person associations with loneliness and positive affect. Relative amplitude showed no association surviving correction. Exploratory indirect associations through social participation were significant for positive affect, meaning and purpose, and self-determination, but not loneliness. None of the 12 cross-level interactions was significant (all ps ≥ .069).
Discussion: Older adults with less fragmented daily activity, characterized by fewer shifts from active to sedentary states, reported higher well-being than their peers. In years when participants were more active than their own usual level, they reported less loneliness and more positive affect. Social participation statistically accounted for part of the between-person associations. These findings are observational and based on a selected subsample.

articles.title: Development and validation of a task for assessing help-seeker relational dynamics.
articles.authors: Tyler Kwan; Jae Shin; Caroline Selai; Orestis Zavlis; Michael Moutoussis
articles.abstract: Self-other evaluations play a crucial role in understanding psychiatric disorders and improving collaboration between service users and providers. However, experimental paradigms of such relational processes tend to have low reliability and ecological validity. Quantitative analyses can validate the task’s measurement properties while qualitative analyses can empower service users to provide novel insights about task development and interpretation. In this study, we use both quantitative and qualitative analyses to develop the “Helping Task” based on the iterated prisoner’s dilemma. In this task, help-seeking participants knowingly engaged in an asymmetric relationship with a computerized help-provider, in which both parties invested effort (points). Initial qualitative feedback from 17 individuals (15 ‘neurotypical’, 2 having lived experience of relational difficulties) was used to refine key task properties (like task instructions, interface labels, and general navigation). Subsequent thematic analyses revealed that these participants interpreted helping exchanges through expectations about reciprocity, moral obligations, and underlying mental intentions, mirroring descriptions of real helping relationships. Moreover, quantitative analyses of 30 online participants validated the task’s sensitivity to helper behaviour and the within-session reliability of mean trust, decision satisfaction, and intended effort. Finally, computational analyses revealed probabilistic states in which trust, decision satisfaction, and effort were jointly lower or higher, indicating that self-other evaluations were linked to willingness to invest in the relationship. These findings support the reliability and validity of the Helping Task and pave the way for computational studies of self-other evaluations in helping relationships.

articles.title: The Map Is Not the Territory: Construct Names, Items, and Responses in Measures of Mentalizing, Epistemic Trust, and Emotion Regulation
articles.authors: Ilaria Maria Antonietta Benzi; Marco Marelli; Laura Antonia Lucia Parolin; Karin Ensink
articles.abstract: Psychology has a measurement problem: different constructs often share the same name, and the same construct is measured under different names. This matters most for constructs theorized as interdependent. In theory, these constructs are defined by name, and their interdependence is posited at that level; in practice, each is measured by a pool of items, often from separate questionnaires, which may overlap or diverge in ways the names do not anticipate. We asked whether construct names correspond to the items that operationalize them, whether items reflect the structure of responses, and whether responses follow the boundaries posited by names or drawn by items. Using reflective functioning, epistemic trust, and difficulties in emotion regulation as a case study, we compared semantic similarities of construct names and items with response correlations in 1,167 emerging adults (aged 18–29, 72% female; item-level analyses preregistered) and 1,068 secondary school students (aged 14–20, 67% female). Construct names best matched their own items in 4 of 11 subscales. Items reflected the structure of responses (r = .62 and .58), also, less closely, across questionnaires (.42 and .37). Responses followed boundaries drawn by items more than those posited by names. A correlation between such measures, usually read as evidence of interdependence, may also arise from items that describe the same experience or from shared method variance. What theory says about a construct thus applies only in part to what its items measure.

articles.title: No evidence that positive outcomes elicit a stronger sense of agency once correcting for publication bias: a commentary on, and re-analysis of, Mariano et al. (2025)
articles.authors: Robrecht van der Wel; Shaheed Azaad; Pernille Hemmer; John Michael
articles.abstract: In a recent meta-analysis, Mariano et al. (2025) conclude that people experience a stronger sense of agency over positive than negative outcomes, indexed by temporal compression. In this commentary, we evaluate that claim and identify several concerns about its validity. First, we argue that temporal compression effects should be standardized before being combined, because values in milliseconds are not necessarily comparable across different paradigms. When we analyzed standardized effects, evidence for a valence effect was absent once adjusting for publication bias. Second, we identified data integrity issues, identifying several studies that were included but either (1) did not manipulate outcome valence at all, or (2) contained only a positive or negative condition compared to a neutral condition. Excluding these studies meant that even unstandardized effects did not support Mariano et al.’s headline finding.

articles.title: A set of dynamical rules for conversational progression act as a precursor to collective cognition
articles.authors: Zachary P Rosen
articles.abstract: Conversation unfolds between speakers as a series of coordinated updates from prior ideas expressed in earlier utterances to new sets of ideas. This process of speakers and conversation partners jointly updating prior "conversation states" is an important piece of the cognitive scaffolding that enables social coordination, and even collective cognition -- the capacity for individuals to pool their cognitive resources to solve problems together. However, a functional data-driven description of how this process works is missing in the extant literature. This report provides a functional description of how conversation states are updated in terms of information-theoretic processes, while analyzing a corpus of 5,447 conversations in nine typologically diverse languages. Our results show that individuals form a strongly connected distributed computational system during conversation, which generates new information according to a power-law distribution. This enables speakers to encode and solve a potentially unbounded number of problems and ideas, simply by conversing.

articles.title: Desinformación y mitos relacionados con la vacunación contra el VPH en Colombia: una revisión rápida de la literatura
articles.authors: Carla Montoya; Christopher Milbert-Beltz; Valentina Grajales; Valery Esteban; Francisco Palencia-Sánchez
articles.abstract:
Introducción: La vacunación contra el virus del papiloma humano (VPH) es fundamental para prevenir el cáncer de cuello uterino y otros cánceres asociados. En Colombia, su aceptación se ha visto afectada por mitos, desinformación y pérdida de confianza, especialmente tras el evento de El Carmen de Bolívar (2014).
Metodología: Se realizó una revisión rápida de la literatura siguiendo la guía metodológica de Cochrane y las recomendaciones PRISMA 2020. Se buscaron estudios en PubMed, SciELO, Web of Science, Embase y Scopus, además de literatura gris; la última búsqueda se realizó en agosto de 2026. Se incluyeron estudios realizados en Colombia y publicados desde 2012 que abordaran mitos y/o desinformación relacionados con la vacunación contra el VPH.
Resultados: Se incluyeron 19 estudios, organizados en tres categorías: mitos, desinformación y consecuencias sobre las tasas de vacunación. Se identificaron preocupaciones sobre la seguridad y eficacia de la vacuna, brechas de conocimiento y creencias relacionadas con la sexualidad, junto con un descenso sostenido de la cobertura desde 2014.
Discusión: La vacilación y negativa a la vacunación son multifactoriales e involucran factores cognitivos, socioculturales e institucionales. La crisis de El Carmen de Bolívar contribuyó a la pérdida de confianza, en un contexto de deficiencias previas en información, comunicación y capacitación. Sin embargo, no se ha establecido causalidad directa entre desinformación y decisiones de vacunación.
Conclusiones: La percepción de riesgo, las brechas de conocimiento y la desinformación continúan siendo barreras relevantes. La cobertura permanece por debajo de la meta de la OMS de 90 % para 2030, y estrategias como el modelo COM-B podrían contribuir a mejorar la aceptación.

articles.title: Avoiding Feelings and Resisting Closeness: A Network Analysis of Attachment and Affect Regulation in Adolescents with Mental Health Concerns
articles.authors: Sherene Balanji; Marlene Moretti
articles.abstract: Adolescents with mental health concerns often experience difficulties navigating attachment relationships and regulating emotions. Although attachment insecurity and affect regulation difficulties are well-established transdiagnostic risk factors for adolescent psychopathology, far less is known about the specific experiences and beliefs that connect these domains. Understanding these connections may provide insight into how attachment insecurity and affect regulation difficulties mutually reinforce one another. The present study used a cross-sectional network analysis to examine item-level associations among attachment and affect regulation in a clinical sample of 608 adolescents (57% female; Mage = 13.98, SD = 2.36) referred to publicly funded youth mental health services. Community detection analyses identified four interconnected dimensions corresponding to attachment anxiety, attachment avoidance, affect dysregulation/suppression, and affect reflection. Notably, affect dysregulation and suppression formed a unified community when examined alongside attachment, suggesting that emotional overwhelm and emotional avoidance may function as closely interconnected aspects of emotional functioning. Two bridge nodes emerged as key points of connection between attachment and affect regulation: the belief that “thinking about my feelings just makes everything worse” and the experience of wanting closeness with a parent while simultaneously pulling away. These findings highlight beliefs about emotions and uncertainty regarding interpersonal closeness and support as important points of connection between attachment insecurity and affect regulation difficulties. Implications for attachment-informed intervention and future research are discussed.

articles.title: A Taxonomy of Misleading Mental Health Content Online
articles.authors: Nicole Bizzotto
articles.abstract: Online mental health communication can mislead without containing demonstrably incorrect claims. This article introduces a taxonomy of misleading online mental health content, distinguishing between source-, message-, and decoding-level misleadingness. It provides researchers, clinicians, and online platforms with a framework for identifying potentially harmful mental health content online that veracity-based approaches may overlook.

articles.title: Expertise Diversity Enhances Information Sharing in Wiki settings: Evidence from Sequential Collaboration
articles.authors: Maren Mayer; Joachim Kimmerle
articles.abstract: Online collaborative projects like Wikipedia rely on sequential collaboration, where individual contributors iteratively revise a shared product. While previous research has examined wikis for collaborative writing and sequential collaboration for numerical judgments, little is known about the cognitive mechanisms underlying information sharing in such settings. The present study bridges research on collaborative writing, group information sharing, and cognitive models of sequential collaboration. Drawing on a computational model of sequential collaboration, we tested whether higher variation in contributors’ expertise facilitates the integration of information into a shared text. In an experiment with 413 participants, we demonstrate that information accumulation increased throughout the sequential chain but at a decreasing rate. Consistent with model predictions, higher expertise variation resulted in more information being incorporated into the shared text. Contrary to expectations, expertise variation did not affect the speed of information accumulation, nor did it increase information deletions. These findings demonstrate that predictions derived from a cognitive model of numerical judgment formation generalize to information-sharing contexts. More broadly, the results suggest that diversity in contributors’ knowledge can improve collaborative knowledge construction in sequential environments. This research adds to evidence that sequential collaboration is an effective mechanism for integrating distributed knowledge in online collaborative systems.

articles.title: Challenging “nature” as a causal category: An environmental bundle approach to restorative experiences
articles.authors: Yannick Joye; Andreas de Block; Dylan Chau Huynh
articles.abstract: Research on restorative environments has long examined the psychological benefits of contact with nature. Findings from this work are often interpreted as showing that nature itself causes restoration. In this article, we provide both a critical assessment of this causal claim, and propose an alternative “bundle” approach. In the first part, we assess whether nature satisfies two requirements for a scientifically useful causal category: coherence and mechanistic relevance. We argue that it remains unclear whether environments classified as natural share a coherent cluster of properties that supports generalization across instances, and whether those properties – such as relative untouchedness or the presence of vegetation and water – are directly mechanistically relevant to restorative outcomes. This lack of clarity has implications for stimulus selection, causal explanation, generalization, and theory development. In the second part, we propose a bundle approach that shifts the units of explanation from the elusive notion of nature to configurations of potentially interacting environmental components that cut across conventionally defined natural and built settings. These components may include low-level perceptual properties, spatial and spatiotemporal relations, affordances, meanings, and social conditions. Integrated with a goal-discrepancy account of restoration, this approach holds that environmental components become restorative insofar as they help resolve an individual’s active situation–goal discrepancies. The bundle approach thus offers an analytical framework for developing more precise, testable, and generalizable explanations of restorative experiences across both natural and built environments.

articles.title: The AI Paradox:  How Optimization May Undermine Meaningful Work in Helping Professions
articles.authors: Matthew J Monnot; Isaac Thompson
articles.abstract:
Helping professions are adopting artificial intelligence (AI) to automate documentation, 
monitoring, and coordination on the premise that offloading routine tasks frees workers for 
meaningful care. That premise assumes managers know which tasks are routine and which 
meaningful. We argue instead for a task-contingent AI paradox: meaning in helping work 
concentrates in identity-central tasks that are increasingly automatable. Study 1, a two-wave 
critical-incident panel of 307 helping-profession workers (144 longitudinal cases one year later), 
tested six pre-specified predictions that Time 1 human-coded meaning dimensions forecast Time 
2 felt meaningfulness, exhaustion, or turnover intentions; estimates were near zero, and 
equivalence at the |β| = .30 sensitivity band held for three of five. One exploratory association 
survived multiplicity screening: narratives grounding meaning in competence were associated 
with higher later turnover intentions and exhaustion (β = .29 and .30, adjusting for six survey 
measures). Automated coding did not reach the human-agreement standard; humans coded all 
predictors. Study 2 coded 7,695 nursing-forum posts captured 2016–2026 for meaning events. 
Nurses named AI in seven events; about one post in twenty per period instead named an 
optimization or implementation object (ratios, metrics, dashboards, documentation load), and the 
facet at issue was control over means. Study 3 found that share unchanged across the decade; the 
one strain marker that rose, lacking control, is confounded with a site template change. No study 
measured individual AI exposure. Against the automation frontier, the results locate the risk of 
optimization in the tasks workers name as meaningful, not in AI as such.

articles.title: Differential effects of individual versus consensus evaluations of narrator-to-story fit on the experience and outcomes of narrative listening.
articles.authors: Carolyn McGettigan; Khadija Faiz; Amy Francis; Elizabeth Leivers; Laurie Sin; Hannah Jones; Nadine Lavan; Saloni Krishnan
articles.abstract: While a reader might imagine the narrator's and characters' voices in a written book, a spoken narrative solidifies the relationship between the narrator and the text. Here, we report two experiments investigating how perceived narrator-to-story fit affects narrative listening enjoyment and other listening outcomes. In a first experiment (N=400 participants), we manipulated the gender-related congruence between the expected and heard narrator of four spoken narratives in a willingness-to-wait paradigm. We found that listeners were more likely to continue listening to congruent than incongruent stories, but did not enjoy them more or comprehend them more accurately. However, we observed a dissociation in the observed effects of perceived narrator-to-story fit: specifically, higher individual evaluations significantly increased enjoyment, while both higher individual and (aggregated) mean fit ratings predicted greater motivation to continue listening. This suggested that crowd-sourced data may be less effective than personal taste when predicting narrative listening enjoyment. Indeed, a second experiment using a larger number of stories showed that participants’ enjoyment of spoken narratives is most strongly predicted by within-sample individual fit ratings, but not by within- or between-group aggregate ratings. Our findings provide evidence to support personalisation of narration as a way to promote enjoyment of spoken narratives and, potentially, audiobooks.

articles.title: Prior information about another’s emotional state shapes the perceptual representation of their facial expressions
articles.authors: Igne Jasukaityte; Margaret Cecilia Jackson; Patric Bach
articles.abstract: Context is known to change how people evaluate facial expressions. However, predictive processing  accounts  claim  that  context  should  also  shape faceperceptual  representation, causing objectively identical expressions to appear different perceptually. We tested thisin five experiments with English-speaking adults in the UK and Ireland,recruited through a university participant pool and online platforms (total N= 413; 18–49 years; data collected 2023–2026).Participants heard how a person was feeling, watched that person’s ambiguous expression change towards a congruent or incongruent emotion, and judged the expression’s final seen emotional state. Expressions were rated as happier after happystatementsand sadder after sad statements (Experiment 1a), replicating prior work. However, they were also rated as more intense when congruent with prior statements than when incongruent (Experiment 1b), ruling out biases from statement-to-response mappings. When participants perceptually compared final  expressions  with  slightly  more  or  less  expressive  probe  faces,  they  generally overestimated faceexpressiveness (Experiments 2a, 2b). Crucially, this overestimation was larger for expressionscongruent with prior expectations, but only when the probe appeared after a longer delay (1000 vs 333 ms). The same pattern emerged when the emotion was not explicitly stated but inferred from a variety of news that participants delivered to the person (Experiment 3). Prior knowledge of another’s emotional state therefore shapes notonlythe evaluation of the person’s facial expressions but also their perceptual representation, consistent with  predictive  accounts.  Generalization  to  naturalistic  expressions,  other  emotions,and cultures remains to be tested.

articles.title: A Relevance Rate Model of the affective mechanisms linking social media use to later attentional disruption
articles.authors: Hippolyte Fournier; eva pool; David Sander; Elise Dan-Glauser
articles.abstract: Social media use is increasingly suspected of harming attention, but the evidence remains too limited to draw any firm conclusions. One obstacle is the lack of a framework specifying how such use might affect attention afterwards, without any device. To address this gap, we draw on emotional attention, the affective mechanism that prioritises what matters to individuals. The Relevance Rate Model rests on the relevance rate, the frequency with which an environment delivers concern-relevant stimuli. Drawing on predictive coding, we suggest that social media raises the rate that users expect, and that this expectation may persist after each session and, with repeated use, across daily life. When an activity delivers less concern-relevant information than expected, sustained attention to the ongoing task may be disrupted as emotional attention is recruited to address the shortfall. The model specifies four measurable parameters of use, from which we derive a research agenda.

articles.title: Tones, Dots and Attentional Biases: An autobiographical account of the development, first implementation, and reception of my attentional-probe paradigm (aka dot-probe paradigm)
articles.authors: Christos Halkiopoulos
articles.abstract: The attentional probe paradigm involves presenting participants with different messages simultaneously through two distinct information channels within the same modality. By measuring reaction times to modality-specific probes that can appear in either channel, this paradigm enables the assessment of attention allocation between these channels. Since the 1980s this paradigm has become prominent for investigating attentional biases in the processing of emotional information. The best-known version of it, the dot-probe technique introduced by MacLeod, Mathews, and Tata (1986), uses the visual modality. What is less well-known is that I had previously introduced the attentional probe paradigm in 1981 in the auditory modality in a modified dichotic listening experiment with pure tones as auditory probes. Using this tone-probe technique this study investigated the contrasting ways in which repressors and sensitisers (Byrne,1961) handle threatening information. Criticisms from a contemporary perspective notwithstanding of the rather limited initial study, it was concluded that sensitisers displayed an attentional bias favouring the processing of threatening stimuli, whereas repressors appeared to avoid the optimal processing of such stimuli.  This paper presents a historical reconstruction of how I developed the attentional probe paradigm, how I first applied it in the auditory modality, and how it was subsequently used in the visual modality. It also introduces a multimodal version to be used in further research and offers a critique of extant research relying exclusively on decontextualized stimuli.

articles.title: Human similarity judgments reveal fine-grained representations of dynamic social scenes
articles.authors: Kathy Garcia; Leyla Isik
articles.abstract: How does the human mind organize dynamic social scenes? Existing accounts rely on pre-defined social-affective or action-based taxonomies, yet whether humans use these dimensions to structure their representations of naturalistic social scenes remains unknown. We collected 53,223 human similarity judgments of videos depicting two-person actions and trained a sparse-positive-embedding model to recover the underlying latent dimensions. These learned dimensions explained twice as much variance in similarity judgments as pre-labeled annotations, captured interpretable fine-grained social-event structure (combining information about social relationships and actions), and fractionated broad semantic content (e.g., separating parent-child interactions into caregiving versus affectionate play). The same dimensions also predicted fMRI responses to passively viewed stimuli across visual cortex better than pre-labeled annotations, highlighting their importance beyond similarity judgments. Together, these results suggest that humans represent dynamic social scenes along fine-grained axes not captured by current taxonomies, and offer behaviorally-grounded targets for future studies of social vision.

articles.title: Noticing yourself perceiving: Embodied reflexivity, experience design, and evidence at a free arts–science exhibition in India
articles.authors: Kohinoor Monish Darda; Hansika Mangwani; Sanjana Edwankar; Sakina Bharmal; Tanvi Raghuram; Siyona Varghese; Samrddhee Pathare; Amisha Keshan; Ritika Deshpande; Sakshi Kharbanda
articles.abstract: This study evaluates Art of Perception, a seven-zone attraction presented at Creative Lab Festival 2026 in Pune, India. A convergent mixed-methods design combined matched pre-post surveys from 200 visitors (166 complete cases) with learning statements, 1,339 face-judgment votes, and 65 post-workshop drawings. Five of six self-report outcomes showed positive paired differences after Holm correction. Bodily relaxation showed the largest difference (22.9 points on a 0-100 scale; standardised difference = 0.69); trust in perception did not differ reliably. Data indicated learning about perception, neuroplasticity, art-brain relations, and nature connection. The observational, immediate, and self-reported design does not establish causation or durability. The paper proposes a public laboratory of perception as a provisional framework for construct-aligned attraction design and evaluation.

articles.title: From Echo Chambers to Echo Machines? Endorsement, Evidence, and the Certainty of Belief in Conversations With AI
articles.authors: Olivier LE BON; Xavier Noël
articles.abstract: Randomized trials show that conversations with large language models (LLMs) can reduce conspiracy belief and, more modestly, political polarization. Yet the same systems can increase conspiracy belief when instructed to, and clinical reports describe chatbot conversations accompanying the escalation of implausible convictions. Prevailing accounts attribute both outcomes to the evidence a model supplies. We note that most experiments confound evidence about the world with endorsement of the person, and that the clearest attempt to separate them favors evidence. Drawing on research on attitude certainty, self-validation, and responses to flattery, we distinguish the position of a belief from the certainty with which it is held and formalize γ, an effect of endorsement on certainty at fixed factual content, interpretable as a validation gain. If higher certainty lowers responsiveness to later evidence, the account permits a conditional outcome: beliefs that become less extreme yet more rigid, without any misinformation. We specify two critical experiments, a factorial test of facts and endorsement that includes a source known to approve everyone and an endorsement-first design with counterevidence held constant, plus an articulation control. Conversational AI becomes a test bench for an old question: can social approval make subsequent evidence matter less?

articles.title: People Expect Less but Show Equal Influence of LLM Versus Human Moral Advice
articles.authors: Neele Engelmann; Eva-Madeleine Schmidt; Ali Alhosseini; Ivar Rodríguez Hannikainen; Mengchen Dong
articles.abstract: People are often skeptical of AI in the moral domain, yet AI-generated ethical advice can influence moral judgments as much as human advice. Unlike most prior work, which attaches human or AI labels to identical advice, we examined how much real advice written by humans and by AI influences moral judgments, and whether people expect less influence from AI than from human advice. First, we developed 24 realistic everyday moral scenarios and collected over 500 persuasive advice texts from both incentivized human writers (N = 92) and GPT-4o. AI-generated advice was longer, more linguistically complex, more semantically uniform, more virtue-oriented, and less extreme than human advice. Next, a new sample of participants (N = 390) either revised initial moral judgments after receiving human or AI advice or indicated how much they expected such advice to influence them. Participants were equally influenced by human and AI moral advice, revising their judgments by a little under a third of the distance to the advice. Participants who only estimated the influence, however, expected less influence from AI than from human advice. These findings suggest that skepticism toward AI in moral contexts may shape people's expectations about AI moral advice, but not how much they are actually influenced by it.

articles.title: “If you don’t vape, it’s abnormal”: Attitudes, perspectives, and perceived functions of vaping and nicotine pouches in Ireland
articles.authors: Rory Coyne; Cheyenne Downey; Mengyang Zhang; Gintare Valentelyte; Paul Kavanagh; Jan Sørensen; Frank Doyle
articles.abstract:
Introduction: Increasing usage of novel nicotine products, including e-cigarettes/vapes and oral nicotine pouches risks proliferating long-term nicotine addiction and adverse health consequences among a new generation. Public health responses are evolving, but need to be informed by a deep understanding of complex and emerging behaviours. While previous research has explored patterns of vaping and nicotine use, less is known about their perceived functions and social meanings. The present study sought to explore attitudes and perceptions of vaping and nicotine pouch use, and the perceived functions that they have among users. 
Methods: This study employed an exploratory, qualitative design, adopting an epistemological stance of social constructionism. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with users of vapes and nicotine pouches aged ≥16 years in Ireland. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. An analytic structure with five themes was generated.
Results: Participants described vaping as a means of managing stress and anxiety, framing vaping particularly as a coping strategy. Nicotine more broadly was constructed as a lifestyle or wellness supplement which supported concentration and productivity. Despite widespread perceived normalisation, participants described feeling ashamed of being a nicotine user. 
Conclusion: These findings show that participants continue to vape and use nicotine pouches not only because of dependency, but also due to perceived emotional, cognitive and lifestyle functions attributed to nicotine. Prevention and cessation efforts are therefore likely to benefit from addressing the perceived functions of vaping and nicotine pouch use, whilst challenging misconceptions surrounding the benefits of nicotine and avoiding stigma associated with nicotine dependency.

articles.title: When the brain can change: effects of neuroplasticity education on beliefs about brain-based mental disorders
articles.authors: Olha Guley; Elena Pasquinelli; Daniel Nettle
articles.abstract: Mental disorders are increasingly framed as brain-based, which can promote pessimism about recovery. We tested whether brief education about neuroplasticity, the brain’s capacity to change throughout life, can counter these beliefs. Across three preregistered vignette experiments with UK adults (Ns = 414, 411, and 418), participants viewed a brain-framed mental disorder after either a brief neuroplasticity video and text intervention or a matched control. The intervention increased the perceived possibility of recovery, but this effect was short-lived after a single exposure in Study 1 and more durable with a booster in Study 2. The effect in Study 3 was not significant, but a pooled analysis of data from Studies 2 and 3 confirmed the positive effect overall. The intervention did not affect perceived treatment efficacy, nor did it reduce desired social distance from people with mental disorders. In Study 3, higher familiarity with the disorder was associated with a higher perceived recovery and lower desired social distance. These findings suggest neuroplasticity education can increase public optimism about recovery from mental disorders, but changing treatment beliefs or social attitudes may require more targeted interventions.

articles_hidden.title: Interpersonal Processes in Daily Life: Loneliness and Social Appraisals as Real-Time Predictors of Non-Suicidal Self-Injury Urges and Behavior
articles_hidden.authors: Michelle Katherine Hiner; Laurence Claes; Brooke A. Ammerman; Olivia J Kirtley; Julie Janssens; Inez Myin-Germeys; Glenn Kiekens
articles_hidden.abstract: Although interpersonal factors are implicated in theoretical models of non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI), little is known about how objective social context and subjective interpersonal experiences contribute to momentary NSSI urges and behaviors in clinical populations. The present study examined between- and within-person associations among several interpersonal processes (perceived rejection, perceived social support, social context, social context appraisals, loneliness) and NSSI urges and behavior in daily life. One-hundred-twenty-five treatment-seeking adolescents and adults with recent NSSI completed a 28-day Ecological Momentary Assessment (EMA) protocol with six daily surveys (15,098 assessments). Dynamic structural equation modeling examined between- and within-person contemporaneous and temporal associations. Higher perceived rejection at baseline predicted greater average NSSI urge intensity and NSSI behavior during the 28-day EMA period, whereas baseline perceived social support was unrelated to either outcome. Momentary objective social context (i.e., being alone versus with others) was not a robust predictor of NSSI urges or behavior in daily life. In contrast, more positive momentary appraisals of social contexts predicted prospective decreases in NSSI urge intensity across 2-hour intervals, while higher-than-usual momentary loneliness predicted within-person increases in both NSSI urge intensity and the likelihood of NSSI behavior. Fully prospective mediation analyses indicated that the temporal effects of loneliness and social context appraisals on NSSI behavior operated primarily through their effect on NSSI urges. Subjective interpersonal experiences, rather than objective social context, were consistently linked to short-term NSSI risk. Interventions targeting maladaptive social appraisals and loneliness, including just-in-time adaptive interventions, may help prevent NSSI urges and behavior in daily life.

articles_hidden.title: The dimensionality and influence of parental attitudes towards childhood multilingualism in Nordfriesland and Fryslân
articles_hidden.authors: Ruth Kircher; Suzanne Victoria Dekker; Jelske Dijkstra; Pavlina Heinzova; Mirjam Vellinga
articles_hidden.abstract: This study examined parental attitudes towards childhood multilingualism in the district of Nordfriesland, Germany, and the province of Fryslân, the Netherlands. Both are home to speakers of the local majority language (i.e. German/Dutch), autochthonous heritage languages (e.g. Frisian), and immigrant heritage languages (e.g. Arabic). Quantitative questionnaire data were collected from 645 parents of young children, making this the first large-scale study of parental attitudes towards childhood multilingualism outside Québec. There were three key findings. First, like in Québec, three evaluative dimensions emerged from parents’ attitudes: status, solidarity, and cognitive development – indicating that these dimensions may characterise parental attitudes across contexts. Second, parents with more positive solidarity-related attitudes were more likely to raise their children multilingually in the home. This is the first time a significant relationship between parental attitudes towards childhood multilingualism and multilingual child-rearing in the home has been attested. Third, no significant attitudinal differences were found between parents in Nordfriesland and Fryslân. The study makes a theoretical contribution by advancing knowledge relevant to attitude theory, and a practical contribution by serving as a basis for research-informed science communication for policy makers and language planners wishing to promote multilingual child-rearing and intergenerational heritage language transmission.

articles_hidden.title: Consensus without a champion: Cross-partisan demand for AI safety regulation in Hungary and the missing belief in delivery
articles_hidden.authors: Gabor Orosz; Janos Salamon; Reza Shabahang; Agnes Zsila; Péter Krekó
articles_hidden.abstract: Industry leaders now ask for independent, pre-release safety testing of frontier AI systems; the US president dismissed such calls as fears about things that “won’t happen.” What the public wants is well documented for the US and UK, but almost unknown elsewhere, and little is known about whether people believe their preference will be acted upon. In a Hungarian online sample (n = 1,356), 75% supported mandatory independent safety testing before AI systems are released, regardless of partisanship. Three in four also believed most Hungarians agree, and 61% believed that this majority was growing. Yet only 32% expected such testing to be introduced. In one of Europe’s most polarized countries, AI safety regulation thus has a consensus but no champion. The missing link is not a hidden majority but the belief that anyone will deliver it.

articles_hidden.title: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Cognitive Bias Modification for Interpretation in Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder
articles_hidden.authors: Daniel Tönsing; Marcel Miché; Johannes Massell; Roselind Lieb; Karina Wahl
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: Cognitive bias modification for interpretation directly modifies maladaptive interpretation biases, central to the development and maintenance of obsessive-compulsive disorder. Although it has been examined across a range of disorders, its efficacy for Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) has not been synthesized.

Methods: A systematic search of Embase, PubMed, and PsycInfo (last search 5 May 2026) identified randomized controlled studies targeted OCD-relevant interpretation biases. The synthesis combines a narrative mapping of design and training parameters, followed by three random-effects meta-analyses for interpretation biases, OCD-relevant beliefs, and OCD symptom severity. Prespecified moderators were training dosage, targeted domain, control condition, and study sample. Risk of bias was assessed with RoB 2 and certainty of evidence with GRADE. The review was preregistered (https://osf.io/n3hbk).

Results: Across 19 studies (N = 1,294), single-session designs predominated in analogue samples and multi-session protocols in the few clinical studies. Cognitive bias modification for interpretation showed a large effect on interpretation biases (g = -0.92 [-1.18, -0.65]), a moderate effect on OCD-relevant beliefs (g = -0.40 [-0.57, -0.22]), and a small effect on OCD symptom severity (g = -0.19 [-0.34, -0.04]). General or mixed training protocols outperformed domain-specific protocols, and symptom reductions were larger in clinical than in subclinical samples. All studies raised some concerns on RoB 2, and certainty of evidence ranged from low to moderate.

Conclusions: We present empirical evidence that cognitive bias modification for interpretation reliably modifies post-intervention interpretation biases, with moderate transfer to OCD-relevant beliefs and small transfer effects on OCD symptom severity, supporting its potential as an adjunctive intervention. The larger effects observed for broader training protocols and in clinical samples highlight that future trials should prioritize clinical samples, multi-session designs, preregistration, and outcome measures that are independent of the training paradigm. Given the few studies per subgroup these findings require replication.

articles_hidden.title: Hidden Neural Variability and the Unexplained Cochlear Implant Outcome
articles_hidden.authors: Kuzma Strelnikov
articles_hidden.abstract: Cochlear implants work, but not equally. After decades of cohort studies, the familiar predictors of outcome (age, duration of deafness, residual hearing, etiology) still leave most of the spread between patients unexplained. Research on how the brain handles degraded speech, audiovisual cues and everyday sounds shows that implant outcome measures test the brain at least as much as the ear. Yet candidacy assessment still examines the cochlea, the auditory nerve and inner-ear anatomy, and rarely the cognitive and structural state of the brain that must learn to use the device. This article argues that undetected neural variability, including cognitive decline, hearing-related atrophy and incidental pathology in brains assumed to be normal, is a plausible and largely unmeasured contributor to the missing variance. It proposes routine cognitive and volumetric phenotyping of implant candidates, and of the control groups against which they are judged. Because the brain restores much of the degraded implant signal through its predictive mechanisms, the article also calls for a new line of work: the development of dedicated tests of predictive brain capacity, a measure currently absent from both candidacy assessment and outcome research.

articles_hidden.title: The orthoblique rotation for factor analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Marcos Jiménez; Mauricio Garnier-Villarreal; Víthor Rosa Franco; Luis Eduardo Garrido; Francisco José Abad
articles_hidden.abstract: The gradient projection algorithm (GPA) is the most used tool to rotate factor models. However, GPA is currently limited to fully orthogonal or fully oblique solutions. Keeping structural zeros in selected positions of the factor correlation matrix after rotation is currently unavailable. This limitation is relevant to analyses where theoretical considerations or study design require certain factor correlations to be zero. We therefore introduce the orthoblique rotation, which allows orthogonal and oblique relations between factors to coexist. Building on Jennrich's algorithms, we describe the geometric foundations of GPA and extend them to the orthoblique rotation. We illustrate its usefulness for exploratory bifactor models with multiple correlated general factors that remain orthogonal to group factors, and for multitrait–multimethod models in which trait and method factors may correlate within their respective sets while remaining orthogonal between sets. Finally, we make available the new orthoblique rotation in the R package latent through the lrotate() function, which extends the capabilities of the popular GPArotation package of Bernaards and Jennrich (2005). Taken together, this work helps bridge the gap between exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses and continues Jennrich's efforts to expand the flexibility and scope of factor rotation.

articles_hidden.title: Neuroscience-Informed Psychoeducation for Sleep Disorders in Psychiatry
articles_hidden.authors: Mohammad Nami
articles_hidden.abstract: Sleep disorders are prevalent among psychiatric patients and are strongly associated with neurobiological, psychological, and behavioral processes. This chapter analyzes neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE), an approach incorporating the insights gained from neuroscience with patient education to understand and manage sleep disturbances better. To establish a scientific basis for psychoeducational interventions, we discuss central mechanisms of sleep regulation such as circadian rhythms, sleep homeostasis, neurotransmitter systems, and brain networks. It illustrates how bidirectional sleep disorders and psychiatric syndromes, including depression, anxiety, PTSD, and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), are linked, and explains sleep disturbance as a transdiagnostic key clinical feature. In addition to cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia, NIPE is used to provide a solution to insomnia by integrating mindfulness-based strategies and personalized interventions with the assistance of digital technologies. Implementation challenges and outcome assessment, as well as ethical dimensions of practice, are also considered. In fact, NIPE is a clinically relevant strategy that can both maximize patient engagement and ameliorate sleep disorder outcomes.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Behavioral Adaptation: Evaluating the Added Value of EEG in Personalized Language Interfaces
articles_hidden.authors: João Fernandes; Carlos Bruno; Luis Ricardo Santos
articles_hidden.abstract: Neuroadaptive interfaces personalize human–computer interaction using brain activity, but whether neural measurements provide useful information beyond behavioral indicators remains unclear, particularly in language comprehension tasks. We propose a framework to investigate the added value of EEG in adaptive communication support. Written messages are presented through combinations of sentence segmentation, pictograms, and keyword labels, with presentation choices informed by individual preferences and task performance. A behavior-adaptive policy serves as the baseline for comparison with a neuroadaptive policy incorporating calibrated EEG estimates under signal-quality and uncertainty constraints. The research plan includes interface validation, behavioral feasibility testing, and an EEG-based comparison using held-out sessions. Evaluation focuses on comprehension accuracy, response time, subjective effort, and adaptation behavior. The objective is to determine whether neural information improves assistance decisions and user outcomes beyond behavioral adaptation.

articles_hidden.title: Neutral minus neutral: Liminal spaces as an uncanny phenomenon of unexplained human absence
articles_hidden.authors: Yuki Yamada
articles_hidden.abstract: Photographs of empty corridors and commercial facilities, known online as "liminal spaces," are judged uncanny by many online viewers. Because most theories of uncanniness locate its cause in the features of humans depicted in the photograph, the appreciation of images that contain no human or animal figures can be used to investigate whether this impression requires a depicted human or whether the expectation that people should be present is sufficient. In a previous empirical study of liminal images, images of rooms from which furniture, doors, and windows had been removed were rated as more than twice as uncanny as the corresponding typical rooms. The effect of human absence, however, has been examined only by replacing human figures with furniture of the same size. Each of four existing accounts, including the structural deviation account, which attributes the impression to deviation from a familiar configuration, explains, on its own, only part of the findings of that study. Here we propose a four-stage model in which uncanniness arises when an observer who judges a place to be in use cannot find a reason for the absence of people or objects that should be there. On the basis of the model, we specify five issues to be tested empirically on which the model and existing accounts make different predictions.

articles_hidden.title: When Unusual Is Usual:  Multivariate Analysis of WAIS-5 Index Score Profiles
articles_hidden.authors: Paul Skirrow
articles_hidden.abstract:
Interpretation of cognitive profiles commonly involves the identification of low scores, discrepancies and relative strengths and weaknesses. However, a finding that is unusual when considered individually may be considerably less unusual within a person's broader cognitive profile. To account for this, Crawford et al. (2012) developed a multivariate approach that placed individual WAIS-IV findings within their wider normative context. The present study extends this approach to the five primary indices of the WAIS-5. 
Monte Carlo simulation of 1,000,000 normative profiles was used to estimate base rates for four complementary aspects of profile interpretation: the rarity of the overall index-score configuration using the Mahalanobis Distance Index (MDI), multiple low index scores, multiple unusual pairwise discrepancies, and multiple relative strengths and weaknesses. Individually unusual findings occurred substantially more frequently when considered across the complete profile, particularly for pairwise discrepancies, where ten overlapping comparisons are possible. The MDI provided complementary information about the rarity of the complete five-index configuration and was more strongly associated with within-profile variability than with overall score level. Together with the accompanying clinical calculator, these analyses provide an accessible framework for placing individual findings and broader patterns of WAIS-5 performance within their normative context.

articles_hidden.title: From defeat to entrapment—and back again: Reciprocal dynamics among constructs from the Integrated Motivational-Volitional model of suicide in young adults
articles_hidden.authors: Neha Parvez; Michael Kyron; Emilia Sherifi; Jeremy Gordon Stewart
articles_hidden.abstract: The Integrated Motivational-Volitional (IMV) model of suicide proposes that feelings of defeat give rise to entrapment, which in turn contributes to suicidal ideation (SI). Although research generally supports this pathway, less is understood about how defeat, entrapment, and SI mutually influence each other over short periods of time. Within a three-week ecological momentary assessment period, we examined short-term temporal associations among defeat, entrapment, and SI (passive and active) in a sample of young adults (N = 156, ages 18-29; data collected 2022-2023) with a recent history of suicidal thoughts or behaviours. We used residual dynamic structural equation models to test concurrent and prospective within-person associations among variables. Higher-than-usual levels of defeat and entrapment were each associated with greater passive and active SI at the same assessment and predicted greater SI at the subsequent assessment. Defeat and entrapment also demonstrated reciprocal associations over time, such that greater levels of each predicted subsequent increases in the other. Similarly, higher-than-usual levels of passive SI predicted subsequent increases in both defeat and entrapment, whereas active SI predicted subsequent increases in defeat only. Findings support the central role of defeat and entrapment in short-term changes in SI. Further, they suggest that the relationship between defeat and entrapment may be reciprocal rather than strictly unidirectional, challenging assumptions of the IMV model. The generalizability of these findings to other age groups and clinical populations remains to be established.

articles_hidden.title: Adolescent Perspectives on Parental Consent Requirements for Depression Treatment: A Mixed-Methods Investigation
articles_hidden.authors: Amanda Smock; Tubanji Walubita; Andy Rapoport; Shannon Hill; Aileen Kangavary; Riley McDanal; Mallory Dobias; Juan Pablo Zapata; Briana Shiri Last; Jessica L. Schleider
articles_hidden.abstract: Depression incidence in adolescents is increasing, yet most do not access treatment. Policies requiring parental consent to initiate care may influence adolescent treatment access. In a convergent mixed methods study, we investigated adolescent perspectives toward accessing treatment with and without parental consent (i.e., self-consent) across four modalities: therapy (in-person and online) and self-guided supports (in-person and online). We explored differences in attitudes amongst sub-samples, demographics, and depression severity. An online survey and qualitative interviews were conducted with 43 adolescents; one sub-sample required parental consent (n = 29), and one self-consented (n = 14) (i.e., parental consent requirements waived). We used a multi-step analytic approach. Using content analysis, we qualitatively coded a positive, negative, or mixed valence to indicate attitudes toward parental consent or self-consent, and calculated frequencies. Using thematic analysis, themes were informed by self-determination theory. Three themes were identified: Factors that Influence Adolescent (1) Autonomy, (2) Competence, and (3) Relatedness. Generally, adolescents viewed self-consent positively, seeing it as preserving their autonomy and decision-making. Self-consent attitudes were consistently positive for self-guided supports and more mixed for therapist-delivered treatments. The ‘waived parental consent’ sub-sample expressed more positive self-consent attitudes overall; younger adolescents described more negative attitudes and adolescents with less severe depression symptoms described more negative and mixed attitudes. Perspectives on parent consent requirements were not monolithic, and were shaped by developmental needs for self-determination. Results suggest supporting adolescents' competence to navigate treatments; preserving autonomy in decision-making; and strengthening parent-teen communication and relatedness to encourage help-seeking.

articles_hidden.title: The Arena Model: An Account of Human Judgment
articles_hidden.authors: Nikolos Gurney
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychology, economics, and behavioral science catalog human judgment through hundreds of disparate cognitive biases. The Arena Model (AM) replaces this disjointed taxonomy with a single account: judgment runs on a low-dimensional projection of a higher-dimensional world. The model derives many canonical heuristics and biases from a few fixed mechanisms. A "bias,'" per the AM account, is what happens when a mind works with fewer dimensions than its environment contains, when a researcher measures dimensions that differ from what the mind used, or when an internal signal is taken to report a property of the world. Many apparent departures from rationality resolve once unmeasured and mismatched dimensions are taken into account. Unlike descriptive frameworks that add a new mechanism for each phenomenon, the AM constrains the space of possible errors and yields clear, falsifiable predictions about the conditions under which biases will and will not appear. It also gives researchers a single, testable account in place of a growing list of unconnected exceptions. I demonstrate consistency across known biases, define the limits of the account, and propose a diagnostic test to evaluate, or invalidate, it.

articles_hidden.title: Neuroscience-informed Psychoeducation for Eating Disorders
articles_hidden.authors: Olivia Chapman; Kira Venables; Abigail Smith; Amanda Makara; Kevin Danaher; Sarah Daniels; Falzah Farooq; Ann Frances Haynos
articles_hidden.abstract: Eating disorders are serious psychological concerns associated with high levels of physical and psychological comorbidity and elevated premature mortality rates. Despite the severity of these disorders, gaps in clinical care exist and most individuals with eating disorders either do not receive or do not benefit from existing evidence-based treatments. There has been a growing movement to incorporate neuroscience-informed targets into eating disorder treatment; however, to date psychoeducation for eating disorders remains narrowly focused on eating- and weight-related behaviors and less directed towards their underlying mechanisms. Yet, neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE) can provide vital insights into diagnostic distinctions, patterns of psychiatric comorbidity, risk and maintenance mechanisms, brain-body relations, prognostic course, and therapeutic targets for eating disorders. Further, knowledge of neuroscience can assist in designing the delivery of psychoeducation with the neurobiology of eating disorders in mind by tailoring content to consider the impact of personality and illness stage on the learning process. In this chapter, we highlight the promise of NIPE for eating disorders, provide a case example of NIPE for eating disorders delivered in a clinical setting, and discuss future directions for research in this area. Ultimately, NIPE can be used to bridge the gap between research knowledge and clinical care in eating disorders, thereby enhancing patient self-efficacy, dispelling misconceptions about eating disorders, and enhancing the accessibility of the science for individuals with these serious, yet undertreated disorders.

articles_hidden.title: The Quantitative Psychologist Is Dead, Long Live the Quantitative Psychologist
articles_hidden.authors: Sacha Epskamp
articles_hidden.abstract:
Much of what quantitative psychologists publish consists of developing statistical methods, implementing them in software, and evaluating them in simulation studies. I argue that artificial intelligence (AI) can already do much of this work, and that its share will only grow. The quantitative psychologist has always been a jack of all trades, combining programming, statistics, and psychological knowledge without being a master of any one of them. AI is now the better jack of all trades. When methods become cheap, value moves to what AI cannot supply and to what it newly makes possible. I describe three directions: collecting trustworthy data from real people, formalizing psychological theory now that computational modeling is within reach of any researcher, and rethinking methodological education
so that students learn to judge the analyses that AI will run for them. The
specialist role built around producing methods for others will fade, while
quantitative thinking spreads through all of psychology.

articles_hidden.title: “Borderline” is likely an “identity” or “emotional” disorder, but definitely not a “personality” disorder: A commentary on Sharp et al. (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Orestis Zavlis
articles_hidden.abstract: In a 17-year longitudinal study, Sharp et al. (2026) report that “self-functioning” outperforms “interpersonal functioning” in predicting later borderline pathology, concluding that the core and distinguishing features of “personality disorder” lie in the “representation of self”. In this commentary, I suggest that these findings can be interpreted in at least two alternative ways. First, I argue that when we take the authors’ findings at face value, we reach the conclusion that (borderline) personality disorder can be understood as an “identity disorder” given that its main impairments lie in “the representation of self”. Second, I argue that when examined closely, the authors’ findings suggest that “(borderline) personality disorder” is an “emotional disorder”, given that the predictor of “self-functioning” is constructed with items that encode emotional, not self-related, pathology. Finally, I conclude by noting that whichever way Sharp et al.’s findings are interpreted, they cannot support the inference that “(borderline) personality disorder” is in any way about “personality”.

articles_hidden.title: How Feminine and Masculine Do Cisgender People in the U.S. Think the Average Gender Nonbinary Person Is?
articles_hidden.authors: Anna Reiman
articles_hidden.abstract: Perception of gender is ubiquitous and consequential in social life. People who are perceived as women are expected to enact femininity, whereas people who are perceived as men are expected to enact masculinity. How do gender nonbinary people fit into these binary assumptions? The present work examined the perceived femininity and masculinity of nonbinary people. In particular, cisgender primarily straight/heterosexual U.S.-based participants reported their assumptions about the assigned sex (Study 1; N = 315) or their perceptions of the femininity and masculinity (Studies 2-3; Ns = 216 and 277) of the average nonbinary person. No apparent bias in terms of assumed sex or perceived femininity emerged, yet participants rated the average nonbinary person as reliably below the scale midpoint on masculinity. Accordingly, straight cisgender Americans’ perceptions of the average nonbinary person may in part reflect a tendency to safeguard masculinity.

articles_hidden.title: Fast or Slow? Individual and Symptom Differences in the Dynamic Speed of Psychopathological Symptoms
articles_hidden.authors: Liying Zhang; Xinchun Wu; Luming Liu; Ying Li; Wenchao Wang; Hao Yuan; Yang Li; Jingmeng Cui
articles_hidden.abstract:
Introduction: Recent research has increasingly adopted complex dynamical systems theory to understand psychopathology. A key proposition is that psychopathological symptoms may operate at different time scales, with different dynamic speeds shaping the evolution of the symptom system. This study examined the extent to which variability in symptom dynamic speed reflects symptom differences, person differences, and person-by-symptom interactions.
Methods: We analyzed five intensive longitudinal experience sampling datasets comprising 265 participants and 33,059 retained observations. Dynamic speed was quantified for each person-symptom time series using lag-1 autocorrelation (AC) and mean period (MP) derived from Lomb–Scargle spectral analysis. Multilevel variance decomposition was used to partition variability into person, symptom, and person-by-symptom components.
Results: Across the two dynamic speed indices, symptom variance was generally non-significant. Person variance and person-by-symptom interaction variance were significant in several datasets and generally exceeded symptom variance, although pairwise differences between variance components were not consistently significant.
Conclusion: The findings provide limited evidence for consistent symptom differences in dynamic speed; person differences and person-by-symptom interactions may play a more prominent role. These results highlight the importance of idiographic approaches to understanding symptom dynamics and underscore the need for further research into the clinical implications of dynamic speed.

articles_hidden.title: Specifying Innateness in Infant Development: A Framework for Theory-Building Based on Co-Determination
articles_hidden.authors: Leher Singh
articles_hidden.abstract: Infant research has often treated early neural and behavioral expression as a privileged window into the initial state of the mind, with early-emerging capacities sometimes uncritically taken as evidence of innate knowledge. This paper evaluates the strength of such inferences through four intersecting lenses: genetics and epigenetics, cultural evolution, definitional precision, and standards of scientific explanation and falsifiability. It distinguishes among several non-equivalent forms of innateness, including claims about representational content, architectural or processing biases, developmental canalization, and maturational timing. In place of broad or underspecified appeals to innateness, it advances co-determination as a framework for theory-building that encourages specification of the biological constraints, experiential inputs, cultural ecologies, developmental timing, and interactive mechanisms proposed to produce a given outcome, as well as the patterns of variation that would support or challenge those claims. The central aim is to provide a more precise and testable basis for theorizing about the initial state of the infant mind.

articles_hidden.title: Brain synchrony between interacting sibling pairs during real-time cooperation: an fMRI hyperscanning study
articles_hidden.authors: Lucia Hernandez-Pena; Arezoo Taebi; Julia Koch; Klaus Mathiak; Lisa Wagels
articles_hidden.abstract:
Siblings typically represent the longest-lasting social relationships. Second-person neuroscience provides a framework for studying the neural mechanisms of real-time, reciprocal social interactions. Yet, most studies have focused on simplified coordination tasks, limited brain regions, and did not investigate neural dynamics between siblings. In the first study investigating brain synchrony between siblings to date, we used fMRI hyperscanning to simultaneously record brain activity in 50 same-sex healthy young adult sibling pairs while they played a complex collaborative problem-solving Tetris game requiring continuous non-verbal complementary coordination. Brain synchrony was quantified using inter-subject correlation across 36 regions of interest (ROIs) of the social brain atlas. 

The interacting sibling pairs showed significantly higher brain synchrony than randomly permuted non-sibling pairs in 19 ROIs (FDR-corrected p < .05). These regions were primarily located within the higher-level theory of mind subnetwork (including bilateral temporo-parietal junction, precuneus and dorsomedial prefrontal cortex), and intermediate-level subnetwork (including anterior insula, inferior frontal gyrus). Greater synchrony in the left temporo-parietal junction significantly predicted better cooperative performance, suggesting that shared neural modelling of a partner's intentions supports effective collaboration. Synchrony in frontal and temporal regions was weakly modulated by cooperative and competitive sibling relationship characteristics; however, these effects did not survive correction for multiple comparisons and should be interpreted cautiously (uncorr. p < .05). 

This study provides first evidence that real-time cooperation between siblings is supported by inter-brain synchrony in core social brain networks. We highlight the value of ecologically valid hyperscanning approaches for investigating neural mechanisms of cooperation in long-term relationships, advancing the field of relational neuroscience.

articles_hidden.title: Suicide imagery subtypes and their relationships with suicide behaviour: a mixed-methods evaluation
articles_hidden.authors: Ann Martin; Cassandra Chakouch; Demee Rheinberger; Peter McEvoy; Julie Lin Ji; Fiona Shand
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: Mental imagery about suicide is a commonly experienced risk factor for suicide, but subtypes and their relationships to behaviour remain largely unexplored. This study aims to identify and describe common themes in suicide imagery content, perceived function, and subjective meaning in relation to suicide behaviour. 
Method: Participants (N=20) provided quantitative and qualitative data about content, perceived function, and subjective meaning across 30 unique instances of suicide imagery via online surveys and semi-structured interviews. 
Results: Framework Analysis resulted in five key themes: (a) Determination imagery depicting a single action script detailing a chosen suicide method, (b) Solution imagery highlighting wanted impacts of suicide, (c) Mental Exercise or fantasy imagery, (d) Discouraging imagery of unwanted impacts of suicide, and (e) Consideration imagery weighing up different methods. Determination and Solution imagery were commonly associated with suicide behaviour. Imagery prior to attempt was often deliberately constructed, wanted, and prolonged (Median duration = 90 minutes).
Conclusions: Findings suggest that imagery themes may vary on dimensions reflecting facilitation and deterrence of behaviour, which may interact to produce ambivalence. In addition to volitional impacts via suicide action script rehearsal, suicide imagery may increase motivation towards suicide. Prior to attempt, suicide imagery may be acceptable, comforting, or even sought after. This study provides a nuanced understanding of suicide imagery subtypes in relation to suicide behaviour and provides a framework to assist clinicians in assessment and formulation.

articles_hidden.title: Information-Seeking Behavior in Mice (Mus musculus) During Visual Discriminations: Evaluating Metacognitive and Alternative Accounts in a Target-Cueing Paradigm
articles_hidden.authors: Kazuhiro Goto; Yuya Hataji
articles_hidden.abstract: Information-seeking behavior is often interpreted as evidence of metacognitive monitoring, but nonmetacognitive factors may also explain such behavior. We examined this issue in mice using a target-cueing procedure in which an information-seeking response produced a hint indicating the location of the rewarded stimulus. In Experiment 1, mice performed an orientation discrimination. In Experiment 2, the same mice performed a grating discrimination in which grating coarseness varied across trials. During training, some aspects of performance were compatible with a metacognitive account. In Experiment 1, information seeking did not increase reliably as the discrimination became more difficult, although hint use improved accuracy most clearly at smaller orientation differences. In Experiment 2, mice sought information more often at lower grating coarseness, and hint use was associated with the greatest accuracy benefit under those more difficult conditions. However, the critical test results did not support the prediction that information seeking would track the need for additional information. Mice frequently sought information in target-only trials, in which no additional information was required, and showed relatively low rates of information seeking in trials in which the initial display consisted of two identical, and therefore nondiagnostic, stimuli. These findings indicate that information seeking in the present task was multiply determined. The observed pattern was consistent with contributions from competition, reinforcement history, and the behavioral utility of the hint. Although some aspects of training remained compatible with confidence-based control, the critical test conditions showed that information seeking was not governed by confidence monitoring alone.

articles_hidden.title: Eliciting Spontaneous Belief-Congruent Action Anticipation in Adults Using Structured Familiarization in Rich Nonverbal Narratives
