articles_hidden.authors: Fumihiro Kano; Josep Call; Nicolas Goppold; Kazuhide Hashiya; Mitsuhiko Ishikawa; Xianwei Meng; Emilie Rapport Munro; Hiroshi Nitta; Yuki Ogawa; Atsushi Senju
articles_hidden.abstract: Humans and other animals predict others’ actions from mental states, even when those states misrepresent reality. The anticipatory-looking false-belief (ALFB) task assesses belief-congruent action prediction without verbal responses, yet its reliability remains debated. Across six experiments, we tested 302 adults using false-belief events embedded in rich nonverbal narratives. We progressively refined familiarization while keeping the critical false-belief induction and test events unchanged. Reliable belief-congruent anticipatory looking emerged after familiarization was restructured, possibly because this reduced reliance on spatial heuristics and encouraged perspective taking. Explicit verbal prediction questions strengthened performance but were unnecessary. The refined procedure was confirmed within the original laboratory and independently replicated in a second laboratory. These findings indicate that belief-congruent action prediction is sensitive to task procedures, especially the predictive structure of familiarization. Our study provides a foundation for evaluating spontaneous theory of mind across development and species.

articles_hidden.title: Psychological preparation in multimodal cancer prehabilitation: a systematic review and meta-synthesis of patients’ experiences
articles_hidden.authors: Michael Baliousis; Aniqa Hussain; Zachary Underwood; Thomas Albert Schroder; Mike Rennoldson; Chloe Grimmett; Hermioni L. Amonoo; Sandy Jack
articles_hidden.abstract:
Introduction: Prehabilitation aims to optimise psychological status, but psychological provision largely addresses existing distress and what preparation for treatment consists of is unclear as prehabilitation services scale up. We asked how patients experience it, what enables or undermines it, and how their circumstances shape what they can use.

Methods: We searched CINAHL, MEDLINE and PsycINFO from inception, last searched 22 May 2026, for peer-reviewed English-language qualitative studies of adults’ experiences of multimodal cancer prehabilitation. Eligible programmes combined at least two of exercise, nutrition and psychological support, and either targeted psychological outcomes or included an element with a stated psychological function; measurement alone did not qualify. Two reviewers appraised reports using the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme checklist plus four domains covering staff training, fidelity, adherence and participants’ words. We synthesised findings by meta-ethnography. No external funding. Registered with PROSPERO (CRD42023434123).

Results: Seventeen reports (2021-2026), predominantly surgical and from six high-income countries, drew on 14 independent samples and 230 patients. Across three constructs and 12 subthemes, patients experienced psychological preparation as having something to act on, discovering what their bodies could do, understanding and managing what was coming, being taken seriously and kept going, and not being alone. These functions arose through exercise, dietary support and relationships with staff and peers, not only explicitly psychological input. Prehabilitation added to preparations already under way. Relevance, timing, burden and continuity after surgery enabled or undermined preparation, depending on patients’ beliefs, capacity, demands and support networks.

Discussion: Evidence came almost entirely from engagers, and staff training, adherence and fidelity were sparsely reported. Psychological preparation did not map onto a discrete component; it arose where what a programme offered matched what a patient could use. Services should build psychological function into how prehabilitation is delivered, who delivers it, and how it is matched to patients.

articles_hidden.title: MASEMiner – AI-Assisted Data Extraction  for Meta-Analytic Structural Equation Modeling
articles_hidden.authors: Ulrich Schroeders; Timo Gnambs; Johanna Einsiedler
articles_hidden.abstract: Meta-analytic structural equation modeling (MASEM) synthesizes multivariate evidence across studies, allowing researchers to examine theory-driven path models, including mediated and predictive effects, and to evaluate the dimensional structure of psychological and behavioral measures. A major bottleneck is the labor-intensive extraction of statistical information from primary studies. Large language models and vision-language models offer new opportunities for extracting such heterogeneous statistics from textual and visual document content. Building on these capabilities, we introduce MASEMiner, an open-source application for AI-assisted extraction and verification of data required for MASEM that can be run locally or accessed through a hosted web interface. MASEMiner supports the extraction of directly reported correlations and related effect sizes as well as indirect information (i.e., factor loadings and factor correlations) used to reconstruct correlation matrices for MASEM. We evaluated MASEMiner in four use cases against human-coded reference databases from published meta-analyses, using separate study sets for prompt development and evaluation. Factor loadings were extracted with near-perfect accuracy (sensitivity ≥ 0.92, precision ≥ 0.98), whereas directly reported effect sizes were recovered completely (sensitivity = 1.00) but with lower precision (0.54–0.69) due to overextraction. In a verification study with four coders, automated extraction plus human verification reduced coding time on average by 42% relative to manual extraction at comparable accuracy. MASEMiner thus supports a human-in-the-loop workflow that reduces manual coding effort while preserving transparency and reproducibility in research synthesis.

articles_hidden.title: A Multi-Regional Study Comparing Perceived Risks between Face-to-Face versus Digital Mental Health Services - Associations with Differences in Preferences and Behavioral Intentions and the Moderation of Self-Construal: A Cross-Sectional Study
articles_hidden.authors: Siu Kit Yeung; Winnie W. S. Mak; Ben C. L. Yu
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background:
Recent studies have investigated preferences and perceptions towards face-to-face and digital psychological interventions. Understanding the potential differences in perceived risks between face-to-face and digital services as well as associations with preferences and intentions, can be worthwhile.
Objectives:
We investigated differences in perceived likelihood of being found out and perceived severity of face loss between face-to-face psychological interventions and digital psychological interventions. We also tested the associations between differences in perceived risks and differences in intentions or preferences towards different types of interventions, and investigated the potential moderation of self-construal, regulatory focus, and cultural background. 
Methods:
We conducted a multi-regional study with 645 college students in Hong Kong China, India, United Kingdom, and Canada. We performed t-tests, correlation analyses, and moderated multiple regressions, while combining with alternative statistical methods to examine robustness and consistency of findings across methods.
Results:
We found that people generally perceive face-to-face interventions to have higher likelihood of being found out and severity of face loss compared to digital interventions, with medium to large effects. While no significant association was found for the difference in perceived likelihood of being found out with the difference in intervention preferences and help-seeking intentions, higher perceived severity of face loss for face-to-face intervention was associated with lower preferences and intentions for face-to-face intervention relative to digital interventions. Such associations are moderated by self-construal but in the opposite direction to our hypotheses, in which people with stronger independent self-construal had stronger negative associations between difference in perceived severity of face loss and difference in preferences or intentions. 
Conclusions:
Our findings contribute by identifying differences in perceived risks between face-to-face and digital interventions as well as association with preferences and intentions. We speculate the surprising self-construal moderation findings may be due to higher reliance on personal feelings and higher prioritization for self-consistency among more independent people, and call for further studies testing such mechanisms. We encourage further much-needed investigations into various forms of perceived risks and potential associations with face-to-face or digital mental health intervention preferences, intentions, and decisions, while examining individual and cultural factors.

Keywords: Digital Psychological Interventions, Face-to-Face Psychological Interventions, Help-Seeking, Risk Perception, Face Loss, Self-Construal

articles_hidden.title: Do young children represent multiple mutually exclusive possibilities?
articles_hidden.authors: Urvi Maheshwari; Caren Walker; David Barner
articles_hidden.abstract: A prominent hypothesis in the literature on logical reasoning suggests that, unlike human adults and older children, 3-year-olds deploy a “minimal representation of possibility” when reasoning about the existence of a reward in one of two possible locations. On this view, children are unable to represent two mutually exclusive possibilities simultaneously, and instead commit to one location for the reward in a pair of possible locations, only considering the second location once they have evidence that their first choice is not correct. Although this hypothesis may explain children’s struggles on various tests of modal reasoning, the idea that children may represent possible reward locations sequentially (rather than simultaneously) has not been directly tested. In two studies, we asked 24- to 38-month-olds to choose two of three reward locations, one of which was physically impossible. We found that children aged 31 to 38 months selected the two possible locations without feedback when required to make a simultaneous choice. We argue that these data are compatible with an ability to represent multiple mutually exclusive possibilities.

articles_hidden.title: Examining the Role of Working Memory in Reasoning and Meta-reasoning:  A Fuzzy-trace approach
articles_hidden.authors: Leili Rouhi; Zuleykha Gasimova; Valerie A Thompson
articles_hidden.abstract: Meta-reasoning, the ability to monitor progress and regulate effort during reasoning, comprises monitoring and control. Monitoring, including confidence, is assumed to guide control processes. Yet, whether monitoring and control compete with reasoning for shared cognitive resources is unclear. To address this, we examined the role of working memory in reasoning and meta-reasoning, drawing on Fuzzy Trace Theory and the meta-reasoning framework. Participants (N = 998) solved syllogisms with and without validity-believability conflict in a two-response paradigm under six constraint conditions. Accuracy declined only when load and deadline were combined. Confidence was lower on conflict than on non-conflict problems and reliably predicted answer changes and rethinking time across all conditions. Monitoring resolution, however, was low throughout. These results suggest cognitive constraints impair reasoning generally but largely spare conflict-detection and control sensitivity. Reasoners’ limited ability to discriminate correct from incorrect responses appears to reflect a general monitoring limitations rather than constrained resources.

articles_hidden.title: Underestimating the replicability of the social and behavioural sciences: an audit of six surprising SCORE replication failures.
articles_hidden.authors: Shaheed Azaad
articles_hidden.abstract: The Systematizing Confidence in Open Research and Evidence (SCORE) project recently published a large-scale replication project within the social and behavioural sciences. The authors replicated only 151 of 274 (55%) claims, a finding covered by major outlets such as the New York Times and Forbes. Here, I audited SCORE replications of six studies where at least one claim surprisingly failed to replicate. These failures were surprising because the original study produced a p < .01 while the replication yielded a significant effect in the opposite direction. I show that, of the 12 claims tested across these six replications, five were miscategorised as failed replications because of data analysis and interpretation problems, and six replications were invalid because of poor data quality and an error in the replication’s experiment code. I conclude that individual replications within replicability projects may benefit from more thorough peer review, and that a more comprehensive audit is necessary before we can be confident in the project’s overall replicability estimate.

articles_hidden.title: The social ecology of development: The changing structure of preschoolers’ everyday experiences at home
articles_hidden.authors: Nele-Pauline Suffo; Anas Suffo; Pierre-Etienne Martin; Yujin Kim; Anam Zahra; Daniel Haun; Manuel Bohn
articles_hidden.abstract: Everyday social interactions shape human psychological development. Research, however, has primarily relied on controlled settings or brief observations; consequently, the nature of naturalistic everyday experiences remains largely unstudied. To address this gap, we developed an automated multimodal processing pipeline to analyze a large egocentric corpus of naturalistic everyday experiences from 107 children aged three to five years in Germany (267.52 hours). The pipeline detects faces, persons, proximity, and speech types to classify time into interacting, available, or alone states. Results indicate a significant ecological reorganization: social interaction dominates at age three and declines towards a more even distribution between states at age six. Conversational agency remains stable throughout preschool, with children sharing it nearly equally with conversational partners. Crucially, social interactions change in their structure in that isolated social cues become significantly less predictive of interactions with age. Thus, preschool social interactions become less frequent but more diverse with development.

articles_hidden.title: Examining Physiological Hyperarousal in the Relationship Between Insomnia and Nightmare Proneness
articles_hidden.authors: William E. Kelly; Ani Enriquez; Faith Yanez
articles_hidden.abstract: Nightmare proneness has been associated with insomnia beyond nightmare frequency and neuroticism. The present study examined physiological hyperarousal as a potential process contributing to this relationship. Participants were 209 adults recruited from a university participant pool and an online community sample. Participants completed self-report measures of nightmare proneness, insomnia, physiological hyperarousal, nightmare frequency, neuroticism, and trauma symptoms. Hierarchical regression and indirect-effect analyses were conducted. After controlling for recruitment source, age, gender, nightmare frequency, neuroticism, and trauma symptoms, nightmare proneness explained an additional 6.5% of the variance in insomnia. Physiological hyperarousal accounted for an additional 2.3% of variance beyond nightmare proneness. Nightmare proneness showed a significant indirect association with insomnia through physiological hyperarousal but maintained a direct association with insomnia after physiological hyperarousal was considered. Physiological hyperarousal may represent one process contributing to the relationship between nightmare proneness and insomnia but does not fully account for this association. The findings support conceptualizing nightmare proneness and physiological hyperarousal as related but non-redundant factors associated with insomnia.

articles_hidden.title: Age-Related Neural Dedifferentiation Is Driven by Declining Reliability
articles_hidden.authors: Tiantian Yang; Molly Simmonite; Ethan Maddox; Bingjie Liu; Thad Polk
articles_hidden.abstract:
Neural dedifferentiation, characterized by reduced distinctiveness of neural representations, is a robust feature of cognitive aging. Multivoxel pattern analyses often operationalize neural distinctiveness as the difference between within-category similarity (reliability) and between-category similarity (confusability). However, it remains unclear whether age-related reductions in distinctiveness are driven by decreases in reliability, increases in confusability, or both, and whether these components demonstrate similar longitudinal trajectories. Using cross-sectional and longitudinal data from the Michigan Neural Distinctiveness (MiND) study, we decomposed distinctiveness into its two components across visual, auditory, and motor cortex in more than 200 young (18-29 years) and older adults (65-94 years) and estimated cross-sectional between-person age differences and longitudinal within-person change simultaneously in mixed-effects models. We found that reliability was lower in older vs. younger adults cross-sectionally, and this reduction was significantly larger than the corresponding effect on confusability. Moreover, reliability also declined longitudinally within individuals across a mean interval of four years. These findings indicate that age-related dedifferentiation is driven primarily by declining reliability rather than increasing confusability, and that reporting distinctiveness alone can conceal substantial age-related change in its components. 
Keywords: Dedifferentiation, distinctiveness, reliability, confusability, aging, longitudinal study

articles_hidden.title: Infants’ Social Evaluations Revisited: An Updated Meta-Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Francesco Margoni; Alvin Wei Ming Tan
articles_hidden.abstract: Over the past twenty years, numerous studies have suggested that infants prefer prosocial agents—who help, comfort, or act fairly—over antisocial agents, who harm others or act unfairly. However, the field has faced replication challenges, including a recent multi-lab failed replication, raising concerns about the robustness of these effects. In response, we updated and extended an earlier meta-analysis, synthesizing 182 effect sizes from published and unpublished studies, with an aggregate sample of 4,089 infants aged 0–32 months, using manual choice and visual preference measures. The estimated meta-analytic raw proportion for infants’ preference for prosocial over antisocial agents was 0.65, 95% CI [0.61, 0.68]. This preference was largely stable across age, type of measure, stimulus format, and scenario type, but there was some evidence that larger studies yielded smaller effects. No clear evidence of publication bias was detected.

articles_hidden.title: Saccade Selection Predictably Changes With Load
articles_hidden.authors: Zakaria Gefferie; Estelle Coelingh; Christoph Strauch
articles_hidden.abstract: Departing from traditional information-maximization accounts, recent work proposes that saccade selection arbitrates economically between the expected benefits and costs of shifting attention. We tested this economic account by manipulating the cognitive resources available during selection, arguing that reduced resources should increase the weight of costs, thereby altering selection. Across two experiments, participants selected between saccade targets while performing a non-spatial memory task that manipulated cognitive load. Targets appeared in directions with previously and independently established intrinsic (effort) costs, quantified through pupillometry. In Experiment 1, monetary rewards were staircased against participants' choices, replicating that money can compensate for intrinsic costs. This yielded an informative reward range from which Experiment 2 sampled randomly. Experiment 2 revealed that higher memory load biased selection toward cost-efficient saccades, while reward sensitivity remained unaffected.Load also selectively shortened the long latency tail, consistent with reduced deliberation under increased load and therefore an increased weight on deliberation cost. Saccade selection thus depends on available cognitive resources, supporting an economic account of visual selection over information maximization accounts.

articles_hidden.title: Music therapists’ attitudes, motivation, and use of treatment manuals: a survey study
articles_hidden.authors: Theo Dimitriadis; Wendy L. Magee; Andrea W.M. Evers; Rebecca S Schaefer
articles_hidden.abstract:
Introduction
Treatment manuals and protocols (TM/Ps) are increasingly used to standardise clinical interventions in music therapy, but they often neglect the motivational needs of clients, which are essential for engagement and recovery. Therapists may, at times, modify or depart from established protocols in order to accommodate clients’ interests, preferences, or motivational needs. This study had two aims: to examine music therapists’ attitudes, practices, and reasons for deviation regarding TM/P use, and to introduce a novel, motivation-driven TM/P targeting a client group where motivation is crucial: clients in the subacute phase after stroke. 

Method
Qualified music therapists (N=93) from five countries completed an online survey addressing demographic background, theoretical orientation, opinions, and behaviour surrounding protocol use, and reasons for deviation. Descriptive statistics were used to summarise the sample; hypotheses were tested using crosstabulations with χ² tests of independence and ordinal logistic regression analysis. 

Results
Music therapists held mixed views on TM/Ps, recognising their value while expressing concerns about impacts on personalisation, spontaneity, and motivation. Many agreed that non-client-focused protocols negatively affect motivation and identified spontaneity restrictions as problematic, though these concerns did not significantly predict actual usage patterns. Usage varied partially by setting (lower in educational contexts), theoretical approach (lower in anthroposophic and attachment-oriented and higher in integrative approaches), and specific attitudes toward TM/P importance, rather than by therapist experience or age, suggesting that contextual factors and individual beliefs about protocol value outweigh demographic characteristics in determining TM/P usage. 

Discussion
Findings highlight the ongoing tension between standardisation and personalisation in music therapy, reflecting shared practitioner concerns. Building on these insights and prior applications, the ReMoCo-IMS Protocol, a motivation-driven TM/P for subacute stroke rehabilitation, is introduced. This protocol advances flexible, evidence-based guidelines that support both clinical rigour and motivational, client-centred care.

articles_hidden.title: Occupational Sex Segregation is Strongly Predicted by Psychological Sex Differences
articles_hidden.authors: Joakim Karl Erik Frostegård; Björn Persson; Kimmo Sorjonen; Kåre Hedebrant; Mikael Lundqvist; Agneta Herlitz
articles_hidden.abstract: If traits of individuals are associated with occupational choice, sex differences in those traits should be associated with sex differences in occupational choice, and consequently, with occupational sex segregation. In this cross-sectional study, we assessed the extent to which this is the case for spatial ability, verbal ability, agreeableness, emotional stability, interest in people and interest in things, across 429 occupations. Participants (N = 2,576, aged 35-45) completed online tests and questionnaires, while students rated occupational requirements. For each occupation, the population sex composition of people with traits in line with requirements was estimated, using trait sex differences and occupational requirement profiles. Estimates were highly predictive of actual population sex ratios, with the model assessing interest and cognition in conjunction explaining the most variance (R2 = .49), followed by the interest model (R2 = .46) and the cognition model (R2 = .18). Among individual traits, sex differences in interest in things were by far the most predictive (R2 = .42). Notably, sex differences in cognition were more predictive of high proportions of men in occupations than high proportions of women. Given lifespan trait stability, these results suggest that cognition and interests matter in occupational choice, with sex differences consequently contributing substantially to occupational sex segregation.

articles_hidden.title: Reading Anxiety in Children and Adolescents and Its Negative Association With Word Reading Performance
articles_hidden.authors: Silvia Siu Yin Clement-Lam; Deborah Anne Schneider-Richardson; Allison Kalva; Celinene M. Lay; Brianna Paquette; Caroline G. Richter; Devin M. Kearns; Fumiko Hoeft
articles_hidden.abstract: Over the past decade, research on reading development and reading disorders has expanded beyond its traditional focus on cognitive-linguistic factors to give increasing attention to socioemotional functioning. The present study leveraged two existing datasets (112 elementary school children aged 7 to 10 years and 110 early-and-mid adolescents aged 11 to 15 years) to examine various dimensions of reading anxiety (RA), including cognitive symptoms, physiological symptoms, and behavioral avoidance, as well as the overall RA effects. Our findings revealed that (1) RA was prevalent among both children and adolescents, although correlations among RA dimensions were stronger in adolescents than in children, (2) higher RA was moderately associated with lower word reading performance in both age groups, (3) no significant differences in RA were observed between children and adolescents or between girls and boys, and effects were not moderated by reading performance, and, lastly, (4) RA was negatively associated with reading performance across levels of reading ability, and this association was not stronger among readers at the lower end of the distribution. These findings reinforce the observed moderate negative association between RA and reading performance in prior research and suggest that RA may affect individuals across reading levels and developmental periods.

articles_hidden.title: Rethinking Consciousness: The Self-Organising Information-Processing Systems Hypothesis
articles_hidden.authors: Jason Robert Potas
articles_hidden.abstract:
Across biology, artificial intelligence and social systems, interacting components develop specialised functions and collective capabilities that were not individually specified in advance. Examples range from reorganised living cells to functionally differentiated neural networks and collective decisions in animal groups. What organisational principles might account for these outcomes—and for consciousness?

We propose the Self-Organising Information-Processing Systems (SOIPS) Hypothesis. Within physical and environmental constraints, causally accessible, information-mediated interactions among changeable components can generate organisational structures that alter subsequent interactions and enable new functions. SOIPS distinguishes a generative engine from Dimension A, describing informational organisation from functional signalling to context-sensitive coordination, and Dimension B, comprising the elementary functional families of retention, inference and regulation. Particular configurations of these elements support composite capabilities, including perception, memory, learning, agency and cognition. Developed capabilities can reshape their own organisational conditions, combine with other functions and contribute to systems at new organisational scales.

Within this framework, consciousness is proposed as a configuration in which awareness-related information participates in flexible cognition. Awareness refers to the organised availability of information about relevant internal or external conditions. Consciousness is thus neither an inevitable endpoint of increasing complexity nor a capability restricted by definition to human biology. If experience is constituted by particular organised neural activity, SOIPS may also help investigate the origins of phenomenal experience.

SOIPS offers a shared language for interpreting biological development, learned organisation in AI and collective behaviour. It also motivates testable predictions: changing information access, constraints or elementary functional contributions should alter the capabilities they support. Cross-domain interventions could assess whether analogous organisational relationships produce comparable outcomes, informing both scientific explanation and the design of artificial agents and institutions.

articles_hidden.title: From Acute MDMA Experiences to Lasting Change: Self-Compassion’s Role in MDMA-Assisted Psychotherapy for Social Anxiety Disorder
articles_hidden.authors: Christina Chwyl; M. Kati Lear; Sunjeev Kamboj; Joanna Arch; Adie Wilson-Poe; Jason B Luoma
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objectives: Self-compassion may benefit individuals with social anxiety disorder and serve as a mechanism of change within 3,4-Methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA)-assisted therapy (MDMA-AT). 
Methods: In this secondary analysis of 20 adults with social anxiety disorder who underwent MDMA-AT for social anxiety disorder (NCT05138068), we examined whether both trait self-compassion changes across treatment (16-weeks) and state self-compassion experienced during MDMA (midomafetamine) dosing sessions contributed to post-treatment clinical outcomes—social anxiety, depression, internalized shame, functional impairment and (thwarted) belonging—beyond baseline levels of each respective variable.
Results: Participants experienced high self-compassion levels during the two dosing sessions. Trait self-compassion increased most substantially after the first MDMA dosing session (ΔM=0.74, p<.001), though continued to increase after dose 2 (ΔM=0.43, p< .001). State self-compassion was not associated with trait self-compassion changes, though explained additional variance in reduced depressive symptoms (ΔR²=.19, p<.001) and internalized shame (ΔR²=.28, p=.02), beyond baseline symptom severity. Trait self-compassion increases following the second dosing session corresponded to reduced internalized shame (β=-.84, p<.001) and thwarted belonging (β=-.68, p=.01), beyond baseline self-compassion levels. Greater baseline self-compassion corresponded to reduced social anxiety, functional impairment, internalized shame, and thwarted belonging (βs<-0.41, ps<.05).
Conclusions: MDMA-AT for social anxiety disorder appears capable of fostering both acute self-compassion experiences and enduring trait-level changes, each of which were associated with certain beneficial outcomes, especially reduced internalized shame. These constructs represent promising candidate mechanisms of change within MDMA-AT for social anxiety disorder, while baseline self-compassion may moderate treatment response,
warranting investigation of self-compassion’s role in future larger psychedelic-assisted therapy trials.

articles_hidden.title: Eye-gaze dynamics reveal the adaptive nature of real-time noisy-channel inference in speech comprehension
articles_hidden.authors: Rachel Anna Ryskin
articles_hidden.abstract: To understand spoken language, listeners must extract meaning from acoustic input that is variable and noisy. The noisy-channel framework posits that listeners overcome this uncertainty by rationally inferring the speaker's intent, combining prior expectations with a model of how the message may have been corrupted during transmission. However, the exact nature of this noise model and its sensitivity to context (e.g., speaker or acoustic environment) remain unknown. Here, I use eye-tracking to measure human speech processing as it unfolds on the millisecond timescale, and I use the representational geometry of a self-supervised speech model (HuBERT) to estimate the noise model. I show that spoken word comprehension is well captured as real-time Bayesian belief updating. Further, listeners flexibly tune their expectation of noise to the specific acoustic environment. These results extend the noisy-channel framework to the moment-by-moment comprehension of speech. More broadly, these findings demonstrate that the human language system continuously adapts its internal model to the statistical structure of the communicative environment. By linking noisy-channel inference with real-time perceptual dynamics, this work highlights the remarkable flexibility of human cognition in navigating uncertainty and opens the door to investigating internal representations in human and artificial speech recognition systems through their fine-grained temporal dynamics.

articles_hidden.title: Object recognition in autism: Shape configuration and Category-specificity
articles_hidden.authors: Christian Gerlach; Esben Helby; Linnea Brønnum Hansen; Ipek Oruc; Mette Elmose
articles_hidden.abstract: Face recognition in autism is well-researched and up to 1/3 of autistic individuals are reported to have severe face recognition difficulties. In comparison, there are few reports on object recognition performance in autism, and the findings are rather inconsistent. Here we report results from a series of object recognition tasks performed by autistic (N = 41) and matched non-autistic participants. Across tasks we varied the demand placed on perceptual differentiation, the structural similarity of the objects, and the salience and value of global shape information (the object’s bounding contour) relative to local shape information (details) in the recognition process. Our main hypothesis was that when local shape information was less salient than global shape information, and when both types of information needed to be integrated to support performance, autistic participants would perform less efficiently than non-autistic participants. This hypothesis was not fulfilled as the autistic group performed just as efficiently as the non-autistic group across all tasks. We discuss our findings in the context of previous reports of object recognition performance in autism and argue that former reports of impairments might reflect lexico-semantic rather than perceptual processes.

articles_hidden.title: Cultural Models of Everyday Love in Contemporary Spain: A Mixed-Methods Cultural Consensus Study
articles_hidden.authors: Saida Heshmati; Jaymes Paolo Rombaoa; Lindy Williams; Dana Hussein; Carmen Goicoechea; Andrew Villamil; Catalina LeeAnn Oselio; Saina Salamati; Corey Abramson; Martín Sánchez-Jankowski
articles_hidden.abstract: Love can emerge through moments and interactions in our daily lives, varying across different cultural contexts. Using a sequential mixed-method approach guided by Cultural Consensus Theory (CCT; Romney et al., 1986), we examined the shared agreement on which daily life experiences evoke loving feelings in Spanish culture across two studies. In Study 1, we conducted semi-structured interviews (n = 54), two-person group interviews (n = 6), and focus groups (3–5 participants; n = 40) to explore how love manifests across different relationships in daily life in Spain. Through qualitative thematic analysis, we identified recurring experiences, centering around explicit affection, instrumental support and dependable care, quality time, and thoughtful, attentive actions. This analysis informed the development of the 61-item Felt Love Questionnaire for Spain (FLQ-Spain), which collects everyday experiences with the potential to make people feel loved within the Spanish context. In Study 2, we administered the FLQ-Spain to a representative sample of Spaniards (N = 502) to assess how likely these experiences are to elicit loving feelings in the Spanish culture. Results from cognitive psychometric analysis revealed a shared agreement in the responses. ‘Highly likely’ loving eliciting experiences were characterized by support and dependability, sharing quality time, and explicit expressions of love—and particularly so within close ties such as family, partners, and friends. Results also showed that controlling or possessive behaviors from romantic partners or familial ties were unlikely to elicit love. This investigation contributes to the understanding of the shared beliefs in love in everyday life based on the perspectives of Spanish culture.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond the Labels: Phenomenological Profiles of Lucid Dreams, Sleep Paralysis, and Sleep-Related Out-of-Body Experiences
articles_hidden.authors: Nerea L. Herrero; Samantha Lee Treasure; Cecilia Forcato
articles_hidden.abstract: Lucid dreams, sleep paralysis, and sleep-related out-of-body experiences (OBEs) are usually defined by a characteristic feature, although considerable phenomenological variability exists within each phenomenon. We explored how different experiential features were organized across participant-level profiles within these phenomena. Data came from an online survey completed by 389 adults who reported at least one of the three experiences. Separate multivariate analyses were conducted within each phenomenon using multiple correspondence analysis followed by hierarchical clustering on principal components. We examined volitional regulation, predominant affective category, and, for OBEs, embodiment-related features. In lucid dreams and OBEs, voluntary induction, agency, and environmental control did not always occur together. Consistent voluntary induction and consistent environmental control characterized different profiles in both phenomena. In OBEs, predominantly positive emotions characterized profiles with different patterns of induction and agency, whereas predominantly negative emotions characterized a profile with low volition. In sleep paralysis, predominantly negative emotions occurred across several phenomenological profiles, whereas predominantly positive emotions characterized a profile associated with vestibular-motor experiences and out-of-body feelings. Sleep-related OBEs also showed marked variability in bodily experience, including profiles characterized by consistent body ownership, variable embodiment, or no perceived body. These findings provide an exploratory description of how phenomenological features are organized across participant-level profiles within lucid dreams, sleep paralysis, and OBEs. The resulting profiles should not be considered fixed subtypes, but rather patterns to be tested in independent samples using prospective or episode-level assessments.

articles_hidden.title: Examining Linking Language and Causal Implications in Observational Psychological Capital Research
articles_hidden.authors: Elise Mockett; Matt N Williams; Dianne Gardner; Larry Paing
articles_hidden.abstract: The present study examines whether the issues with implied causal inference identified by Haber et al. (2022) in observational health research extend to the field of industrial-organisational (IO) psychology. Haber et al. found that causal relationships were implied through the language used to link exposures and outcomes and through recommendations for action. This small-scale conceptual replication applies Haber et al.’s approach to psychological capital (PsyCap), an increasingly popular construct in the domain of IO psychology. Specifically, we evaluate the causal strength of the language used to describe the nature of the connection between given variables when reporting findings and when making recommendations for action in 50 PsyCap articles. The majority of action recommendations were found to have strong causal implications (85% in abstracts, 84% in discussion sections), and most linking sentences implied some level of causality (64% in abstracts, 58% in discussion sections). This was despite very few articles explicitly stating an intention to estimate causal effects (10%) and many explicitly warning against drawing causal inferences (42%). No significant relationship was found between the causality implied in the linking sentences and the strength of causal implication of the action recommendations. These findings have important implications for how research is implemented, and very real consequences for those who are the focus of such implementations. Increased transparency about causal interests and reasoning is needed to uphold the credibility of findings and the integrity of applications of observational PsyCap research.

articles_hidden.title: Extending the Validation of the Anhedonia Scale for Adolescents into Young Adulthood: Psychometric Properties and Longitudinal Prediction of Depressive Symptoms
articles_hidden.authors: Sena Demir-Kassem; Katie Prizeman; Angad Sahni; Xueqing Ma; Manasa Veluvali; Tarun Vermani; Samantha Catherine Cacace; Ciara McCabe
articles_hidden.abstract: Anhedonia is a core symptom of depression linked to poorer outcomes in young people. The Anhedonia Scale for Adolescents (ASA) is a 14-item multidimensional measure validated in 11–18-year-olds. We examined its psychometric properties in 1,199 individuals aged 16–25 years, with and without clinical diagnoses. Confirmatory factor analysis supported the original three-factor structure over one- and two-factor alternatives. Internal consistency was excellent for the total scale (α = .92), acceptable to good for the subscales (α = .71–.88) and comparable across age and clinical groups; five-month test–retest reliability was moderate (ICC = .69). The ASA correlated with the Snaith–Hamilton Pleasure Scale (SHAPS; rₛ = .66) and depressive symptoms (rₛ = .80), explained variance in depressive symptoms beyond the SHAPS (ΔR² = .32), and predicted depressive symptoms five months later beyond baseline symptoms. The ASA is a reliable, valid measure of anhedonia across adolescence and young adulthood.

articles_hidden.title: Imagining, fast and slow: Dissociating reference-frame speed and content speed in mental simulation
articles_hidden.authors: Hanbei Zhou; Ash Bu; Tomer David Ullman
articles_hidden.abstract: Research on the imagination has examined how changing the contents and spatial framing of a mental scenes changes that scene. But hardly any work has changing the \textit{temporal} reference frame of the imagination. For an ideal simulator, changing the frame-rate in which something is imagined should not matter for scene content, but it is unknown whether changing the temporal frame affects people's imagination. Across three studies and six experiments (N = 223 after exclusions), participants watched stylized and naturalistic scenarios  of projectile and pendulum motion at different playback speeds, and continued them in their mind. Our set-up dissociates temporal reference frame from content speed, which allowed us to compare people's predictions to simulation models that do or don't separate content from temporal frame. We found that participants could adjust their imagined temporal reference. Participants also kept content separate from reference-frame speed in realistic (but not stylized) scenes.

articles_hidden.title: Thematic structure and pause duration shape event segmentation during speech listening in younger and older adults
articles_hidden.authors: Yulia Lamekina; Ryan Panela; Carolyn Kortje; Ingrid Johnsrude; Bjorn Herrmann
articles_hidden.abstract: Event segmentation – the division of continuous experience into meaningful units – is essential for understanding narratives. Yet little is known about how listeners segment auditory stories, how prosodic cues such as pauses contribute, and how age-related changes in hearing and cognition affect this process. We conducted two experiments to address these questions. In Experiment 1, human and advanced AI voices for audiobooks and podcast monologues produced longer pauses at thematic event boundaries than within events, indicating that pause timing aligns with narrative structure. In Experiment 2, younger (19–35 years old) and older (56–79 years old) adults listened to stories in which pauses were selectively prolonged at event boundaries or event centers. Older adults identified event boundaries more frequently overall. Prolonging pauses at event boundaries did not enhance boundary identification, whereas prolonging pauses at event centers led to boundary identification despite the absence of a major thematic shift, particularly in listeners with poorer hearing. Hence, aging may change the sensitivity to event boundaries during continuous speech listening, and pause duration can bias event segmentation when thematic cues are absent.

articles_hidden.title: The gender gap in math anxiety (and in the link between math anxiety and math achievement) is not so salient when other anxieties are controlled for
articles_hidden.authors: Monika Szczygieł; Mateusz Hohol
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background and Objectives: Math anxiety (MA) is considered to affect math achievement and the choice of math-related educational paths, thus contributing to the gender gap in STEM careers. However, despite decades of research, the mechanisms underlying the relationships between gender, MA, and math achievement remain largely unclear. One of the reasons is that different types of anxiety and math achievement levels are rarely controlled for.
Design and methods: We tested the associations between gender, MA, spatial anxiety, test anxiety, neuroticism, and math achievement in a sample of 269 adults. 
Results: We replicated previous findings that spatial anxiety in areas of navigation and mental manipulation, but not imagery, mediates the relationship between gender and MA. Importantly, in light of previous contradictory findings, we found that math achievement significantly mediated this relationship. Crucially, we found that gender, spatial anxiety, test anxiety, neuroticism, and math achievement together accounted for 66% of the variance in MA, with gender uniquely accounting for only 5%. 
Conclusions: The commonly reported gender gap in MA is less pronounced when other anxieties are controlled for, especially given that we did not observe gender differences in the strength of the relationship between MA and math achievement.

articles_hidden.title: Suppressing Distractors, Enhancing Targets: Template Tuning in Ensemble Perception
articles_hidden.authors: Gizem Tanseli Kaspar; Sabrina Hansmann-Roth
articles_hidden.abstract:
Abstract
Ensemble perception is a fundamental mechanism enabling the visual system to rapidly extract summary statistical properties (e.g., mean orientation) from a large number of objects. This study investigated the influence of attentional templates for targets and distractors which are formed during visual search, on subsequent ensemble perception. Participants first completed a visual search task involving target and distractor colors, followed by an ensemble orientation estimation task in which these colors recurred in various combinations. The first experiment revealed that target template systematically biased ensemble estimates, with the strongest effect occurring when both template colors recurred together. Furthermore, on these trials the bias exceeded the sum of the individual effects of target and distractor conditions, which demonstrates that combined effect of target enhancement and distractor suppression may be greater than predicted by their individual effects. In the second experiment, presentation duration (150 ms vs. 500 ms) was manipulated. While our results showed that duration did not alter the magnitude of the biases, a longer presentation time improved response precision. These findings suggest that ensemble perception can be modulated by recently formed attentional templates and systematically shape the formation of summary statistical representations.
Keywords: Ensemble Perception, Attentional Templates, Statistical Summary Representations

articles_hidden.title: Procedural learning in the serial reaction time task in individuals with and without Dyslexia: group-level and individual differences
articles_hidden.authors: Catia Margarida Oliveira; Marianna E. Hayiou-Thomas; Lisa Henderson
articles_hidden.abstract: An impairment in the procedural memory system, responsible for the extraction and assimilation of regularities from sensory input, has been suggested to play a causal role in neurodevelopmental disorders such as dyslexia. In this study, we compared the performance of adults with and without dyslexia on the Serial Reaction Time task across three sessions. Alongside it, this experiment presents the first examination of the stability of procedural learning in a dyslexic population. Across sessions, there was no evidence of an impairment in the dyslexic groups, thus lending no support to the procedural deficit hypothesis. There was limited evidence for a relationship between language/literacy abilities and procedural learning, with only a significant association between nonword repetition and procedural learning for the dyslexic group (r = .31). However, given that the reliability of the SRTT was well-below adequate psychometric standards in both groups, the lack of correlations between these measures may reflect attenuation. Nonetheless, a positive correlation between attention and procedural learning was observed in both groups, suggesting that individuals with better attentional abilities showed more evidence of procedural learning in the SRTT (rs between -.34 to -.47). In light of these findings, it is unclear whether a procedural learning impairment can account for the behavioural and cognitive profile observed in individuals with dyslexia.

articles_hidden.title: Common psychiatric treatments alter affective dynamics
articles_hidden.authors: Quentin Dercon; Quentin JM Huys; Robb Rutledge; Camilla Nord
articles_hidden.abstract: Affective states are dynamic, fluctuating in response to recent events: an unexpected pleasure, a disappointing loss. Affective biases, which cause disruptions in these dynamics, are core components of mental ill-health, but the specific effects of treatments on these biases are poorly understood. Here, we investigate the impact of common psychiatric treatments on subjective assessments of happiness, confidence, and engagement during a reinforcement learning task (N=935; 130 taking antidepressant medications). Half (N=459) of the participants were randomised to practice a common psychotherapeutic technique—cognitive distancing—throughout the task. From a joint computational model of learning and affect, we find evidence for distinct and overlapping impacts of psychiatric treatments on affective dynamics. Cognitive distancing attenuates downward drift in happiness and engagement and increases recency bias in the affective impact of recent choices. Conversely, antidepressant use increases baseline happiness and confidence in individuals with similar levels of current symptoms, and decreases recency bias such that more past events influence affective states. Crucially, both cognitive distancing and antidepressant use converge to dampen negative biases in happiness and confidence specifically in participants experiencing higher levels of anxiety and depression symptoms. Together, our results indicate that common treatments for mental ill-health may alter symptoms through their impact on affective dynamics, but via distinct mechanisms.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond referral: Making physical activity opportunities usable in school-based social prescribing for young people experiencing loneliness
articles_hidden.authors: Robert J Booth; Nano Quirke-Bakradze; Sophie Ellis Cooper; Daisy Fancourt; Daniel Hayes
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: For young people experiencing loneliness or low community connection, physical activity may support social contact, enjoyment and belonging. Social prescribing offers a person-centred route to organised sport, exercise, active recreation and less structured movement, but identification or referral does not ensure usability. Little is known about the individual, relational, school and community conditions that make these opportunities meaningful to the young person, workable within their circumstances and acceptable in their social and emotional context.
Methods: A targeted qualitative content analysis with iterative framework development used data from INcreasing AdolesCent social and community supporT (INACT), a school-based social prescribing programme for pupils experiencing loneliness or low community connection. 38 interviews were screened (12 young people, eight parents/guardians, five school staff and 13 link workers); 37 contained physical-activity material. These were analysed alongside link-worker records for 163 young people. Material was charted by activity category, setting, pathway stage, barriers and inclusion or emotional-safety considerations, then compared across pilot interviews, full-trial interviews and logs. Three researchers contributed to coding, checking and collective interpretation.
Results: Across interviews and routine records, physical-activity material encompassed organised sport, fitness and exercise, dance and creative movement, outdoor activity, informal movement or active recreation, and other community activities. Five overlapping areas of work were identified: understanding interests and personal fit; expanding activity options; supporting access and entry; working through practical feasibility and sustainability; and considering inclusion and emotional safety. These areas were not sequential and could overlap or be revisited. School settings interacted with family routines, peer cultures and community provision to shape usability. Logs more often documented named activities, practical actions and spending, whereas interviews provided fuller accounts of confidence, social fit and family constraints. Pathway stages from discussion and referral to attendance and continuation were not consistently distinguished.
Conclusion: For pupils experiencing loneliness or low community connection, access to a potentially connecting physical activity depended on more than availability or referral. The framework describes the practical, relational and contextual work involved in moving towards meaningful, workable and acceptable participation. It locates responsibility across families, schools, providers, services and local infrastructure while keeping young people’s preferences and choices central. The study does not establish that physical activity reduced loneliness, but provides a basis for prospective evaluation of participation, social connection and loneliness outcomes.

articles_hidden.title: Maternal Anxiety and Depression, Parenting, and Child Social-Emotional Functioning as an Interconnected System: Network Evidence from Born in Bradford
articles_hidden.authors: Bradford Mental Health Research Centre BMHRC; Emre Deniz; Eleanor Jane Bryant; Paul Sullivan; Cara E Staniforth; Reena Uddin; Paul Tiffin; Ruth Wadman
articles_hidden.abstract: Maternal emotional wellbeing and children’s social emotional functioning are closely related. Parenting may play an important role in this relationship, as mothers and children respond to one another’s emotions and behaviours in everyday family life. However, we know less about which specific maternal emotional symptoms, parenting characteristics, and child social-emotional functioning are interconnected within a broader family emotional system. We explored these relationships in 5,143 mother-child dyads from Born in Bradford, a large, ethnically diverse cohort in the United Kingdom. Children were approximately 9 years old and mothers approximately 38 years old. Using cross-sectional psychometric network analysis, we examined the structure connecting maternal depressive and anxiety symptoms, parenting characteristics (e.g., efficacy, affection and strictness), and five domains of children’s social-emotional functioning (i.e., emotional difficulties, peer problems, conduct problems, hyperactivity/impulsivity, and prosocial behaviours). Four distinct but interconnected communities emerged, representing maternal depression, maternal anxiety, parenting, and child social-emotional functioning. Maternal worry-related anxiety symptoms and difficulty relaxing were particularly strongly connected within the overall network, while conduct problems were the most strongly connected child domain. Parenting characteristics, particularly strict parenting, were prominent in connecting maternal and child domains. Together, our findings highlight the value of understanding maternal symptoms, parenting, and child functioning within a broader family emotional system. We propose that interventions may be most effective when they address these two areas together, for example by supporting parental worry and child conduct problems within a shared family-focused approach.

articles_hidden.title: Bounded and Unbounded Number Line Estimation in Adults: Accuracy, Response Characteristics, and Mathematical Achievement
articles_hidden.authors: Felix Ayesu; Sharon Henry Yakusi; Valentine Ampah
articles_hidden.abstract:
Number line estimation is widely used to examine numerical magnitude processing and its relationship with mathematics. However,
it remains unclear whether mathematical achievement is more closely associated with estimation accuracy or with characteristics of
estimation responses. The present study examined these relationships among 192 adults who completed bounded and unbounded
number line estimation tasks and mathematics assessments covering arithmetic, fractions, algebra, and percentages. Linear,
logarithmic, mixed log-linear, proportional judgment, and scallop models were compared to characterize estimation responses. We
also evaluated the relationships of estimation accuracy and fitted-response characteristics with mathematical achievement. Linear
models best predicted bounded estimation, whereas mixed log-linear and selected scallop models offered small improvements
for unbounded estimation. Greater linearity and stronger proportional judgment model fit were associated with greater bounded
estimation accuracy, while mixed log-linear characteristics were related to estimation error in both tasks. Bounded estimation accuracy
was more consistently associated with mathematical achievement than unbounded accuracy. Most fitted-response characteristics
accounted for little additional variation in mathematics after considering estimation accuracy, although exploratory analyses indicated
that mixed-model characteristics contributed modest additional information. The findings highlight the value of distinguishing
estimation accuracy from the mathematical characteristics of estimation responses when investigating individual differences in
mathematical achievement.

articles_hidden.title: Post-Encoding Semantic Processing Produces Systematic Distortions in Episodic Memory
articles_hidden.authors: Katelyn G. Cliver; Kennedy N King; Alexa Tompary
articles_hidden.abstract: How new experiences can update a memory has important consequences for its long-term storage, but little is known about how different kinds of re exposure may differentially influence its content. Inspired by theories of memory reconstruction that posit that memory retrieval depends on the integration of idiosyncratic details and relevant general knowledge, we investigated how exposure to a memory through category- or item-level processing may strengthen its episodic and semantic components. Across three behavioral experiments, participants encoded image-location associations in a protocol designed to generate a conflict between memory for specific images and knowledge of the general location of other images from the same category. Following learning of the locations, participants completed manipulations aimed to prioritize category-level or item-level processing of the images. We hypothesized that requiring semantic processing after learning would reinforce prior category knowledge associated with each image and increase category-driven distortions in memory at test. Our findings revealed that memory for images that underwent semantic processing were less precise and more distorted relative to memories that underwent item-level processing and relative to those that were not re-exposed after encoding. Furthermore, post-encoding manipulations more strongly updated memories of atypical category members, suggesting that the organization of prior knowledge can govern the extent that new memories can be updated. Together, these results highlight the active role of post‑encoding manipulations in differentially reshaping memory content and provide compelling evidence that episodic memory retrieval is a constructive process that integrates across prior knowledge, discrete experiences, and subsequent re-exposure.

articles_hidden.title: Does the Variance of Personality Traits Change Across the Lifespan? A Meta-Analytic Review of Longitudinal Studies
articles_hidden.authors: Peter Haehner; Susanne Buecker; Marco Altorfer; Vera Bocklet; Wiebke Bleidorn
articles_hidden.abstract: Although personality traits are relatively stable compared to other constructs, comprehensive meta-analyses have shown that the mean-levels and rank-orders of personality traits change throughout the lifespan. In contrast, relatively little is known about whether and how the variance of personality traits develops with age. Examining changes in personality trait variance is, however, critical to contextualize knowledge on mean-level changes, to identify disruptive life phases, to evaluate the changes in predictive utility of personality traits, and to advance personality development theories. The present meta-analysis thus integrated research from 362 longitudinal studies (Ntotal = 398,124) to identify changes in personality trait variance across time and age. We found remarkable stability of personality variance for all traits, indicating that, at the population level, people neither get more different nor more alike across the lifespan. The only deviations from this pattern were variance increases in neuroticism during late childhood and early adolescence (5 to 14 years) and variance decreases in extraversion during middle and late adulthood (45 to 80 years). Notably, though, effect sizes differed substantially across studies and measures. Our results provide novel insights into the lifespan development of personality traits that can be used to advance theoretical frameworks and inform practical applications. Furthermore, by providing benchmark values for the comparison of effect size estimates of future studies (https://personalityresearch.shinyapps.io/VarianceChange/), we aim to facilitate more systematic and cumulative research on variance changes in psychological traits.

articles_hidden.title: Longitudinal Dataset of Psychological Variables Influencing AI Perception and Usage
articles_hidden.authors: Angelica Lermann Henestrosa; Gerrit Anders; Nico Ehrhardt; Anna Christina Faller; Nora Hampel; Irena Vanessa Ivan; Stefanie Helene Klein; Teresa Luther; Mike Prentice; Busra Sarigul
articles_hidden.abstract: Since the emergence of large language models (LLMs) in 2022, generative artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly expanded into mainstream applications, leading, for example, to the integration of Apple Intelligence into customer devices in 2024. This integration into personal technology marks a significant shift and a further reduction in barriers to use, bringing advanced AI capabilities into everyday devices and making them accessible to private individuals. Thus, the use of generative AI along with interaction through LLM-powered (voice) assistants and engagement with AI-generated content is expected to increase significantly. However, data that link this usage to psychological variables and shed light on the underlying mechanisms of this use over time remain scarce. In this longitudinal study, data from a US-American sample was collected across six waves at two-month intervals between September 2024 and July 2025. It examines user behavior, attitudes, knowledge, and perceptions related to generative AI. Thus, this dataset allows for future research on psychological and behavioral dynamics of AI usage over time, offering insights into user engagement and the individual factors connected to it.

articles_hidden.title: Validating the Big Five Aspect Scales (BFAS) and the Short Form (BFAS-40) in German, French, and Italian
articles_hidden.authors: Peter Haehner; Michael Dominik Krämer; Wiebke Bleidorn; Christopher James Hopwood
articles_hidden.abstract: Personality traits predict health, well-being, relationship success, and work-related outcomes, but most of the relevant evidence comes from English-speaking populations. The Big Five Aspect Scales (BFAS) are one of the most used English-language personality questionnaires, allowing to assess Big Five domains and aspects validly and reliably. In the present study, we validated German, French, and Italian translations of the BFAS and its short-form (BFAS-40) in a representative sample of Swiss adults (N = 4,492). Across the three languages, the translations of the BFAS and the BFAS-40 showed satisfactory psychometric properties in terms of their factorial validity, reliability, and convergence of short- and long-version. Furthermore, we found partial weak measurement invariance across the three languages for all aspects and domains and strong invariance for some aspects. Finally, in line with existing research, aspects belonging to the same Big Five domain differed in their associations with external variables like political orientation and life satisfaction. The translations of the BFAS and the BFAS-40 may thus facilitate future research on personality traits in non-English speaking samples.

articles_hidden.title: A Systematic Review and Theoretical Framework of Stress Generation in Daily Life
articles_hidden.authors: Peter Haehner; Rosalie Andrae; Wiebke Bleidorn
articles_hidden.abstract: Stress generation describes processes by which individuals actively contribute to the occurrence of self-generated stressful events. Personal characteristics like neuroticism or psychopathology have been found to predict the occurrence of major life stressors over several months or years. However, a profound understanding of stress generation over shorter time periods in people’s daily lives is still missing. Here, we integrated recent research on person-environment transactions from personality psychology into the clinical stress generation literature to develop a process model of stress generation. This process model posits that stress generation unfolds across multiple timescales and that short-term dynamics between momentary, state-level personal characteristics and daily hassles are the building blocks for established long-term stress generation effects. To evaluate a core aspect of this model, we conducted a systematic literature search on stress generation in daily life (45 studies, Ntotal = 9’818). Results show that both dispositional traits and momentary states predict the occurrence of daily hassles, supporting the existence and relevance of stress generation in daily life. However, future research on stress generation across timescales is needed to test the theorized link between stress generation in daily life and long-term stress generation effects.

articles_hidden.title: A Smartphone-Based Intervention to Decrease Neuroticism: Protocol of the CHILL Study
articles_hidden.authors: Peter Haehner; Amanda Jo Wright; Rosalie Andrae; Till Lubczyk; Leyla Anina Rosero Betancourt§; Christopher James Hopwood; Wiebke Bleidorn
articles_hidden.abstract: Many people worldwide want to be less neurotic. As lower levels of neuroticism predict a range of positive life outcomes, including health, work success, and relationship quality, interventions that help people to become less neurotic could have wide ranging impacts. This study protocol describes the rationale and design of the CHILL Study (Changing How I Live Life) that aims to evaluate the effects of a smartphone-based intervention to reduce neuroticism in the general public. The CHILL Study comprises four survey assessments spread over 5 months, a 6-week intervention phase, and two 1-week experience sampling phases without interventions. During the intervention phase, participants who wanted to become less neurotic were randomized to four different treatment groups. These treatment groups differed in the employed intervention strategies that target different aspects and levels of neuroticism. The CHILL Study moves beyond existing research on volitional personality change by testing which strategies most effectively decrease neuroticism and evaluating the longevity and generalizability of intervention-induced neuroticism change via peer-reports, implicit personality assessments, and a 7-week follow-up period. The goals of the CHILL Study are to generate an effective method for decreasing neuroticism and facilitating the development of a comprehensive theory of neuroticism change.

articles_hidden.title: Personality Predictors of Health, Well-Being, Relationships, and Employment in Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa: A Three-Year Longitudinal Study
articles_hidden.authors: Peter Haehner; Catherine Mkaleso Shirima; Marie-Christin Kura; Luzelle Naude; Christopher James Hopwood; Amber Gayle Thalmayer
articles_hidden.abstract: Personality traits have been found to be robust predictors of important life outcomes. However, evidence on longitudinal personality-outcome associations stems almost exclusively from Western countries. It is not yet known if, how, and to what extent personality traits are robustly linked to life outcomes in sub-Saharan Africa. Using data from the Africa Long Life Study, which sampled young adults from Kenya, Namibia, and South Africa (N = 2,770), we examined the Big Two personality traits, agency and communion, as predictors of seven life outcomes (self-reported health, life satisfaction, depression, anxiety, employment status, relationship status, financial situation) 2 to 3 years later. We used specification curve analysis to examine the robustness of personality-outcome associations. Higher levels of agency and communion robustly predicted higher levels of self-rated health and lower levels of anxiety and depression over 2 to 3 years. Furthermore, higher levels of communion predicted being employed 2 to 3 years later. However, personality-outcome associations were smaller than previously observed in Western countries (.02 ≤ |r| ≤ .11) and depended on analytic decisions such as country and the time lag between assessments. Our findings provide novel insights into the cross-cultural replicability of personality-outcome associations.

articles_hidden.title: Ten Concerns About Personality-Change Interventions—and How to Address Them
articles_hidden.authors: Peter Haehner; Eva Asselmann; Saskia Baumgardt; Lena Brüggmann; Jaap J. A. Denissen; Claudia Harzer; Christina M. Juchem; Michael Dominik Krämer; Niclas Kuper; Lara Puhlmann
articles_hidden.abstract: Many people want to change their personality in some way and personality traits have been found to predict various important aspects of life, including well-being, health, relationship quality, and work success. As a result, volitional personality interventions designed to elicit personality trait change in desired directions have recently gained momentum in research and public discourse. Although the initial evidence on the effectiveness of these interventions is promising, concerns regarding their benefits, risks, and societal implications remain underexplored. In this review, we discuss 10 concerns regarding methodological, ethical, and practical limitations of volitional personality change interventions. Drawing on research across different areas of psychology, we provide a balanced discussion of each concern and outline directions for future research and practical applications of these interventions. Volitional personality change interventions have the potential to improve people’s life and increase satisfaction with the self. However, realizing this potential requires sustained research efforts, thoughtful study design, and careful implementation of these interventions to maximize benefits and mitigate concerns.

articles_hidden.title: Individual Differences in Personality Trait Changes Across the Lifespan: A Meta-Analysis of Longitudinal Studies
articles_hidden.authors: Peter Haehner; Christopher James Hopwood; Lukas Schellenberg; Ted Schwaba; Wiebke Bleidorn
articles_hidden.abstract: Recent meta-analyses and large-scale longitudinal studies have shown that the mean-levels and rank-orders of personality traits change throughout the lifespan. However, people differ from each other in their patterns of personality development. These individual differences in personality trait changes provide important insight into the sources and course of personality development. The present meta-analysis quantified the magnitude of individual differences in personality trait changes and their fluctuation across time lags and age by integrating findings from 229 longitudinal studies (N = 230,492). Results indicated significant individual differences in change in all traits, with neuroticism showing the most pronounced differences, and openness and agreeableness the least. Charting effects across the lifespan, individual differences in change were most pronounced in childhood, decreased during young adulthood, but were significant across the entire lifespan. The age at which individual differences in change were smallest varied across traits, from ages 30 to 75. Finally, individual differences in personality trait changes were larger over longer assessment intervals, for facet-level traits, and among measures that were not designed to examine the Big Five taxonomy. Our findings support theoretical claims that highlight the relevance of genetic and environmental sources of personality development and suggest that individual differences in change endure, challenging the predictions of set-point models of personality development. Moreover, our results provide benchmarks for individual differences in change that can be used to compare the magnitude of differential personality development in future research.

articles_hidden.title: Questionable mediated effect of self-management on athletic performance: A comment on Fan et al. (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen
articles_hidden.abstract: Drawing on the covariance matrix reported by Fan et al., I reassessed the empirical basis of their mediation model linking self-management to athletic performance. I demonstrate that the observed covariance structure can be reproduced by a theoretically different latent-variable model that does not rely on the directional mechanism proposed in the original article. In this alternative account, self-reported self-management, psychological resilience, competitive spirit, and athletic performance are conceptualized as indicators of a broader construct, core self-evaluation. The results illustrate a broader inferential problem in psychological research: multiple theoretically plausible models may provide equally adequate explanations of the same correlational pattern. Consequently, observational associations alone offer limited grounds for preferring one explanation over competing alternatives. Researchers should therefore routinely evaluate alternative models when drawing inferences about psychological mechanisms from nonexperimental data.

articles_hidden.title: Stress Generation Across Hours, Days, and 1 Month
articles_hidden.authors: Peter Haehner; Lukas Schellenberg; Michael Dominik Krämer; Amanda Jo Wright; Wiebke Bleidorn; Christopher James Hopwood
articles_hidden.abstract: Stressful events can trigger mental health problems. Mental health problems, in turn, predict the occurrence of stressful events—a phenomenon called stress generation, which can initiate detrimental cycles between stress and mental health. However, existing research has focused on long-term stress generation. Here, we aimed to advance the understanding of how stress generation unfolds across different timescales by combing experience sampling, daily diary, and 1-month longitudinal data (N = 403). We found that between-person differences in depression, rumination, reassurance seeking, and neuroticism were linked to the occurrence of daily hassles over hours and days and major life stressors over a month. Furthermore, momentary neuroticism and rumination prospectively predicted the occurrence of daily hassles over several hours. Finally, some indicators of hourly and daily stress generation prospectively predicted the occurrence of major life stressors. These findings provide the starting point for a thorough understanding of how stress generation unfolds over time.

articles_hidden.title: Event-Related Changes in Personality Traits, Life Satisfaction, and Mental Health: Evidence from a 4-Year Longitudinal Study in sub-Saharan Africa
articles_hidden.authors: Peter Haehner; Tracy-Ann Adonis; STEPHEN ASATSA; Maria Florence; Tasneem Hassem; Daniel Hofmann; Christopher James Hopwood; Marie-Christin Kura; Sumaya Laher; Luzelle Naude
articles_hidden.abstract: Life events like entering a romantic relationship or losing a job have been found to predict changes in personality traits and well-being. However, findings on event-related changes stem almost exclusively from Western countries. Here, we address this limitation by examining event-related changes in agency, communion, life satisfaction, and mental health among young adults living in Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa (N = 3,928). A finding that converged with prior meta-analyses from Western contexts was that childbirth predicted decreases in agency whereas event-related changes in other events diverged substantially from findings in Western samples. For example, finishing education or getting a driver’s license predicted decreases in agency and communion. Furthermore, having first sexual intercourse was associated with decreases in mental health. Future cross-cultural research is needed to test potential explanations for why event-related changes differ across cultural contexts.

articles_hidden.title: Working at a Cost? ADHD Symptoms, Self-Endangering Work Behavior, and Occupational Well-Being
articles_hidden.authors: Kerstin Erdal; Johanna Kreft; Johanna Finnemann
articles_hidden.abstract:
Self-endangering work behavior (SEWB) describes strategies employees use to maintain occupational functioning despite potential costs to health and recovery. This study examined associations between attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), SEWB, and occupational well-being using variable- and person-centred approaches.
Participants were 471 working adults in Germany; 176 met the ADHD criterion based on self-reported diagnosis and/or a positive Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale screen. Group differences across ten SEWB dimensions and associations with burnout, work engagement, and perceived stress were examined. Latent profile analysis identified configurations of continuous ADHD symptoms and SEWB.
Participants in the ADHD group reported higher levels across all SEWB dimensions (ds = .20–.78). SEWB dimensions showed differentiated associations with occupational well-being, with little evidence that these associations differed by ADHD group.
