Four ADHD–SEWB profiles differed across all well-being outcomes but did not reproduce categorical ADHD group membership.
ADHD-related characteristics may represent one person-level correlate of SEWB, while substantial heterogeneity exists in how ADHD symptoms and SEWB co-occur and relate to occupational well-being. Findings should be interpreted considering the cross-sectional design, highly educated sample, and ADHD classification based on self-report and screening.

articles_hidden.title: Age-related changes in strategy use during reinforcement learning
articles_hidden.authors: Irene van de Vijver; Leendert van Maanen
articles_hidden.abstract: Age-related declines in reinforcement learning (RL) are commonly attributed to impairments in dopaminergic prediction-error learning and working memory. However, successful RL may also depend on discovering and applying higher-order learning strategies that reduce memory demands. We investigated whether age differences in RL partly reflect reduced spontaneous strategy discovery, whether providing support attenuates these differences, and whether these effects depend on stimulus verbalizability. Sixty younger and 59 older adults completed an RL task in which stimulus-response mappings either contained no underlying structure or could be grouped according to semantic or visual regularities. Across four phases, participants received increasingly explicit information about these regularities. Strategy use was assessed using verbal reports and by fitting sigmoid functions to individual learning curves, estimating the transition to strategy-based responding. Older adults showed lower learning performance, reported using strategies less frequently, and transitioned later to strategy-based responding than younger adults. Providing structured stimulus-response mappings and increasingly explicit information improved learning performance, increased reported strategy use, and accelerated strategy discovery in both age groups, with the largest performance gains observed in older adults and for concrete compared to abstract stimuli. Verbal fluency predicted both learning performance and strategy discovery. These findings suggest that age-related differences in RL reflect not only declines in associative learning but also reduced spontaneous discovery and application of effective learning strategies. Facilitating strategy discovery may therefore represent a promising way to improve learning in older adulthood.

articles_hidden.title: Conspiratorial echoes of disease: The relationship between pathogen prevalence and conspiracy beliefs
articles_hidden.authors: Maciej Siemiątkowski; Maciej Górski; Michał Bilewicz; Theofilos Gkinopoulos; Brian W. Haas; NA; Mohsen Joshanloo; Paul Shing-fong Chan; Ari Nowacki; Efisio Manunta
articles_hidden.abstract: Conspiracy beliefs vary substantially across countries and regions, yet the ecological factors underlying this variation remain largely unexplored. Drawing on behavioral immune system theory, which suggests that pathogen threat can heighten vigilance toward potential dangers, we examined whether pathogen prevalence predicts conspiracy beliefs. Study 1 analyzed four cross-national datasets (20-32 countries) and found that conspiracy beliefs were higher in countries with greater historical pathogen prevalence. Study 2 tested this relationship in a preregistered study using a larger sample (N = 15,503 from 55 countries) and found that historical pathogen prevalence predicted higher levels of conspiracy beliefs. Study 3 extended these findings to the US state level using data from 123,781 participants across 50 states. Finally, Study 4 (N = 493) experimentally manipulated perceived pathogen prevalence and found causal effects on generic and vaccine-related conspiracy beliefs. These findings extend behavioral immune system research by relating pathogen-rich ecologies to contemporary conspiracy thinking.

articles_hidden.title: Urban Aesthetics: Beauty and Interestingness of the City
articles_hidden.authors: Joerg Fingerhut
articles_hidden.abstract:
This paper develops an empirically informed aesthetics of the city by introducing interestingness as a
complementary category to beauty. While beauty has long defined architectural value through
harmony and rightness, urban life also requires experiences of dissonance, openness, and surprise.
Contrasting Scruton’s notion of architectural beauty with Mumford’s conception of the city as secular
and dramatic, I side with Mumford’s more open understanding of urban life.

Conceptually, I propose a middle way that neither centers exclusively on beauty nor simply endorses
a pluralist aesthetics of the city, as is common in contemporary philosophy of the city. To capture the
psychology of urban life, I focus on aesthetic emotions that help explain the experiences of beauty,
interestingness, and belonging. Methodologically, I likewise argue for a middle way that combines
philosophical reflection with empirical research on the psychology and neuroscience of the built
environment. Taken together, the paper outlines an urban-theoretical framework that understands
urban public space, in particular, as an aesthetic interface linking perception, affect, and cognition to
forms of civic participation. Beauty provides coherence; interestingness sustains vitality. Together,
they define the aesthetic and psychological livability of the city.

Keywords
Aesthetic emotions; Affordances; Beauty; Empirical aesthetics; Interestingness; Neurourbanism,
Urban Aesthetics

articles_hidden.title: Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients and spectral features directly drive micro-level autonomic reflexes during brief respiration practices
articles_hidden.authors: Jung-tzu Chang; Zai-Fu Yao
articles_hidden.abstract:
While digital health platforms increasingly deliver guided mindful breathing interventions via audio, the specific acoustic properties of the guidance are fundamentally ignored as potential active ingredients. This within-subject study implemented an unprecedented high-density experimental design to investigate how distinct, computationally engineered acoustic features (e.g., pitch, zero-crossing rate, natural background sounds) modulate acute cardiovascular, respiratory, and autonomic responses. To rigorously eliminate sex-related physiological variance, 21 meditation-naïve female university students completed 13 randomized audio sessions of a standardized 4-minute-and-5-second guided breathing practice (yielding 273 high-density recording epochs). Multiparametric biosignals, including pulse rate variability (PRV), respiratory dynamics, and electrodermal activity (EDA), were continuously recorded. Results demonstrated a robust reduction in blood pressure independent of audio conditions, confirming the fundamental efficacy of a single bout of spontaneous breath awareness. However, high-resolution analyses revealed a highly modular architecture where peripheral
autonomic indices (EDA and PRV) were acutely sensitive to fine-grained acoustic features, specifically Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs). Furthermore, physiological coupling patterns reorganized dynamically depending strictly on the acoustic context. These indings fundamentally challenge the assumption that meditation audio is a neutral delivery medium, establishing acoustic parameters as potent, independent modulators of human autonomic reflexes for future digital therapeutics.

articles_hidden.title: Speech Monitoring During Self-Comprehension
articles_hidden.authors: Andreas Lind; Petter Johansson; Lars Hall
articles_hidden.abstract: Spontaneous speech is full of false starts, rephrasing, and speech errors. Speakers’ ability to detect errors and other problems in their own speech is commonly explained by monitoring mechanisms that rely on pre-articulatory representations, production states, or derivative predictions. We develop an alternative, cue-integrative account in which verbal self-monitoring is a natural consequence of what we have previously termed self-comprehension: speakers’ integration of contextual and sensory information to understand their own unfolding speech without requiring that meaning or intention be fully specified before articulation. Two sources of anticipatory information are central to the account, neither requiring explicit predictive or forward-model representations. First, we apply to self-comprehension the recently proposed idea of multi-scale pattern completion during speech comprehension, which allows partial input to activate continuations at multiple linguistic levels, generating contextually constrained anticipation. Second, anticipatory coarticulation can provide auditory and somatosensory information about upcoming speech before the relevant segment is produced, challenging the assumption that sensory feedback is too slow for online self-comprehension. We propose three routes to error detection: divergence between pattern-completion-based and coarticulatory anticipations; divergence between pattern-completion-based anticipation and post-articulatory sensory feedback; and post-articulatory self-comprehension in the absence of sufficiently informative anticipation. These routes provide a framework for explaining error detection across the observed range of error-interruption latencies, including very rapid interruptions. This framework also provides alternative interpretations of error-detection findings under noise-masked auditory feedback and of cortical attenuation during speaking without requiring a separate pre-articulatory monitoring channel, explicit predictions, or prediction-error computations.

articles_hidden.title: Culturally embedded affect: A grounded theory of recursive eco-emotional processing in young adults in Nepal and India
articles_hidden.authors: Samridha S J B Rana; Paul Graham Morris; Emily-Marie Pacheco
articles_hidden.abstract:
The climate and ecological crises disproportionately affect communities from low-and-middle-income-countries, yet to date most studies of eco-emotions have been with Western populations. This study sought to investigate the views and experiences of young adults in Nepal and India regarding emotional responses and coping to the ecological and climate crises. 

Using constructivist grounded theory, interviews were conducted with twenty-four young adults, equally split between region (Delhi national-capital-region in India, and Kathmandu Valley in Nepal); poor and middle-class urban populations; and male/female sex, to ensure a suitable range of experiences. 

The grounded theory model proposes that eco-emotional experiences are initiated by lived ecological disruption, such as air pollution, heat, and environmental degradation, rather than via abstract knowledge of climate change. These disruptions are then interpreted through culturally embedded meaning systems, including religious practices, agricultural rhythms, and place-based identity, and are further shaped by structural inequalities, such as socioeconomic positioning and perceived political inaction. 

Eco-emotions emerge not as discrete states but as dynamic configurations, in which anxiety, anger, sadness, grief, hope, and helplessness coexist and fluctuate. Perceived agency operates as a key interpretive dimension influencing emotional trajectories. Where agency is experienced as viable, distress may be channelled into problem-focussed or meaning-focussed coping. Where agency is constrained, coping shifts towards strategies that regulate distress through psychological distancing, including fatalism, resignation, and disengagement. Coping processes recursively reshape how ecological disruptions are interpreted over time. 

This framework situates eco-emotions within the intersection of ecological change, cultural meaning-making, and structural inequality, offering a contextually grounded account of their emergence and regulation.

articles_hidden.title: Do people believe diet impacts physical and mental health? Development and validation of the Diet-Health Belief Scale (DHBS)
articles_hidden.authors: Jane Brealey; Joanna Brooks; Zoé Colombet; Rebecca Evans; Eric Robinson
articles_hidden.abstract: Diet can impact on physical and mental health, but to what extent do people believe this? Health psychology theory proposes that beliefs about the impact diet has on health likely shape behaviour. Yet, diet-health beliefs have not been systematically studied and methodology used in existing research is limited. This two-part study aimed to explore UK adults’ beliefs about the impact diet has on short-term and long-term physical and mental health conditions, and to conduct initial development and validation of a scale to measure diet-health beliefs. An initial 20-item scale was completed by a general population sample of 399 UK adults online. Results show that participants had inconsistent beliefs about the impact diet has on long-term and short-term physical health outcomes. Participants tended not to believe that diet impacts mental health. Next, exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis of survey responses indicated a 15-item two factor (physical health, mental health) scale provided the most statistically appropriate measure of diet-health beliefs. The scale was found to be reliable at both full (ωₜ = 0.93) and subscale level (factor 1: physical health, ωₜ = 0.90, factor 2: mental health, ωₜ = 0.93). Convergent, divergent and test-retest validity assessments confirmed the scale had acceptable validity. The scale could be used to investigate whether beliefs about the impact of diet on health shape dietary behaviour and investigate the effectiveness of interventions designed to change diet-health beliefs.

articles_hidden.title: Understanding what works in school food policy: A multistakeholder approach to quantify policy
articles_hidden.authors: No authors listed
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Most children do not meet nutrition recommendations. Primary schools are a key setting for improving children’s healthy eating, yet overlapping policy guidance can make it difficult for schools to determine which food policies to adopt. Research is needed to quantify which policy components are most effective, feasible, and tailorable to school and child needs, and to identify the mechanisms through which they influence behaviour.
Methods: A multistakeholder approach was taken: 1) consultation with food policy experts to provide insights and feedback about the project; 2) scoping of policies across England and Wales to identify effective policy components and the potential mechanisms by which policies may be working to improve healthy eating; 3) engagement sessions with stakeholders (school staff) and end-users (children) in primary schools in Birmingham, UK; and 4) triangulation of insights gained. Fourteen individual policy components were identified. Each component was quantified using indicators of effectiveness (expert opinion; empirical evidence), feasibility (child endorsement; staff views; financial and resource demands), and opportunity for tailoring. Theoretical mechanisms were mapped to each policy component to demonstrate core pathways. 
Results: Scores varied across components. ‘Learning about food’, ‘role modelling’, and ‘eating with others’ ranked highest across indicators, while components such as ‘growing food’ and ‘preparation or cooking food’ were limited by cost and resource demands. Five components had limited or no empirical evidence despite perceived feasibility. Twelve components were rated as having moderate to high potential for tailoring to school and child needs. Six mechanisms were identified (exposure, food accessibility, motivation, social influences, and knowledge- and skills-based food literacy), each mapping onto multiple policy components. 
Conclusion: This study provides a comprehensive framework for understanding the effectiveness, feasibility, and opportunity for tailoring school food policy components, alongside the mechanisms through which they may operate. Findings offer practical guidance to support schools and policymakers in selecting and tailoring policies to diverse contexts. Further research should test the proposed mechanisms and explore how tailored approaches can improve healthy eating for all children.
